records.greek: Καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα περιεπάτει ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐν τῇ Γαλιλαίᾳ, οὐ γὰρ ἤθελεν ἐν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ περιπατεῖν, ὅτι ἐζήτουν αὐτὸν οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι ἀποκτεῖναι.
records.gloss: And after these things was walking the Jesus in the Galilee; for not he was wanting in the Judea to walk, because were seeking him the Jews to kill.

L.1: And after these things Jesus was walking about in Galilee, for He did not want to walk about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill Him.

R.1: After this, Jesus traveled around Galilee. He did not want to go around Judea, because the Jewish leaders there were trying to kill Him.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the religious authorities in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: They are the ones already seeking to kill Jesus in 5:18, and the same aim returns in 7:19 and 7:25. That is the leadership, not the people of Judea as a whole: Jesus, his brothers and his disciples are Jews, and the crowds in Jerusalem are divided about him (7:12).

decisions.choice: he did not want (SBLGNT)
alternatives: he did not have authority (a few witnesses)
decisions.reason: The reading of almost all manuscripts is "he did not want" to travel in Judea. A few witnesses, among them Codex Washingtonianus (W) and some early Latin copies, read "he did not have authority" (that is, he was not free) to travel there. The change may have come from a wish to show that Jesus was not avoiding danger out of fear. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: was walking about: a period of travel in Galilee, some months long
decisions.reason: The tense describes an ongoing ministry from place to place. "After these things" covers a gap: chapter 6 took place near Passover (6:4), in spring, and the Feast of Tabernacles (7:2) came in autumn, about six months later. The verb "walk" is used again for Judea, so the two regions stand side by side.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}, {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:his|His}}, {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}}, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}}, {{deity_pronoun:yourself|Yourself}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Christ uses the deity_pronoun setting, including "me" and "my" when Jesus speaks of himself and "you" and "your" when his brothers speak to him. At the start of a sentence "He" or "My" is written plain. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders there
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote. "There" ties them to Judea, where Jesus is not going.

records.heading: Jesus and his brothers

records.greek: ἦν δὲ ἐγγὺς ἡ ἑορτὴ τῶν Ἰουδαίων ἡ σκηνοπηγία.
records.gloss: Now was near the feast of the Jews, the Tabernacles.

L.2: Now the feast of the Jews, the [Feast of] Tabernacles, was near.

R.2: It was almost time for the Jewish Festival of Shelters. For a week each year, people lived in shelters made of branches. This helped them remember how God cared for Israel in the desert.

decisions.choice: Tabernacles: the autumn festival when Israel lived in shelters
decisions.reason: The name σκηνοπηγία means "the setting up of tents" or shelters. The Law commanded Israel to keep the festival for seven days in the seventh month, after the harvest of grain and grapes had been gathered in, and to live in shelters of branches to remember that God made Israel live in shelters when he brought them out of Egypt (Leviticus 23:33-43; Deuteronomy 16:13-15; Nehemiah 8:14-17). It was one of the three festivals when men were to go up to the place God chose (Deuteronomy 16:16), so Jerusalem filled with pilgrims. It was a joyful feast. Jewish writings from soon after the New Testament (the Mishnah, tractate Sukkah) describe water being poured out at the altar and great lamps lit in the temple courts during the festival; Jesus's words about living water and light in 7:37-38 and 8:12 are spoken at this feast.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the Jewish people, whose festival it was
decisions.reason: As at 2:13, 5:1 and 6:4, John names the festival as the people's, for readers who did not keep it. Jesus and his brothers are Jews and go up to keep it (7:10).

decisions.choice: Tabernacles (L, B); Festival of Shelters (R)
decisions.reason: "Tabernacles" is the long-established name of the festival and is kept at Literal and Balanced. In current speech "tabernacle" mostly means the tent of meeting, so Readable uses the plain word "shelters". Balanced says "festival" for the feast, as at 5:1 and 6:4.

decisions.choice: For a week each year ... cared for Israel in the desert
decisions.reason: Readable says what the festival was, as 6:4 does for Passover (meaning decision m1). The reason given is the one Leviticus 23:43 states.

records.greek: εἶπον οὖν πρὸς αὐτὸν οἱ ἀδελφοὶ αὐτοῦ· Μετάβηθι ἐντεῦθεν καὶ ὕπαγε εἰς τὴν Ἰουδαίαν, ἵνα καὶ οἱ μαθηταί σου θεωρήσουσιν σοῦ τὰ ἔργα ἃ ποιεῖς·
records.gloss: Said therefore to him the brothers of him, "Move from here and go into the Judea, so that also the disciples of you will see of you the works which you do;

L.3: So His brothers said to Him, "Move on from here and go into Judea, so that Your disciples also will see Your works that You are doing;

R.3: His brothers said to Him, "You should leave here and go to Judea. Then Your disciples there can see the things You are doing too.

decisions.choice: brothers: the brothers of Jesus named in 2:12
decisions.reason: The word is the ordinary one for brothers; specific men are meant, and Mark 6:3 names four of them (James, Joses, Judas and Simon). Christians differ on who they were: younger sons of Mary and Joseph, sons of Joseph by an earlier marriage, or close relatives such as cousins. The text does not settle it, so every level says "brothers".

decisions.choice: your disciples: followers of Jesus in Judea and Jerusalem
alternatives: the disciples who had turned back in 6:66
decisions.reason: Jesus had gained many followers in Jerusalem and Judea before (2:23; 3:22-26; 4:1), and the brothers speak as though they need to see him at work there. Another view is that they mean the disciples who had stopped following him (6:66), who might be won back by a public show. The text does not say which.

decisions.choice: the brothers urge a public display at the festival
decisions.reason: The festival was the time when the crowds would be in Jerusalem (7:2). The brothers want Jesus to do his works where they will be seen and win him a following. John explains in 7:5 that they did not believe in him; their advice is like the crowd's wish to make him king (6:15), a way of being great that Jesus refuses.

decisions.choice: there (B, R); the things you are doing (R)
decisions.reason: "There" makes plain that the disciples meant are those in Judea (meaning decision m2). Readable says "the things you are doing" for "your works", here and at 7:7, so the link between the two verses stays in plain words.

records.greek: οὐδεὶς γάρ τι ἐν κρυπτῷ ποιεῖ καὶ ζητεῖ αὐτὸς ἐν παρρησίᾳ εἶναι· εἰ ταῦτα ποιεῖς, φανέρωσον σεαυτὸν τῷ κόσμῳ.
records.gloss: For no one anything in secret does and seeks himself in openness to be; if these things you do, reveal yourself to the world."

L.4: For no one does anything in secret and himself seeks to be [known] openly. If You do these things, show Yourself to the world."

R.4: People who want to be known do not hide what they do. If You are doing these things, show Yourself to the whole world."

decisions.choice: openly: in public view, known to everyone
decisions.reason: παρρησίᾳ means openness: speaking freely and plainly, or acting where all can see. Here it is set against "in secret". The word runs through the chapter: no one speaks openly about Jesus for fear (7:13), and then he teaches openly in the temple (7:26). Elsewhere it means plain speech (10:24; 11:14; 16:25, 29), and at his trial Jesus says he has spoken openly to the world (18:20).

decisions.choice: show yourself to the world: make yourself known to the public
decisions.reason: The verb φανέρωσον means to make visible or reveal. John uses it of Jesus revealing his glory at Cana (2:11), and the brothers mean something similar but on their own terms: a public display. The same root returns in 7:10, where Jesus goes up not publicly but as it were in secret, and the phrase "in secret" is repeated there as well.

decisions.choice: the world: people at large, the public
decisions.reason: In the brothers' mouth "the world" means everyone, all who will be in Jerusalem for the feast. Jesus answers in 7:7 with the darker sense of the word: the world that hates him.

decisions.choice: if you do these things: granting that he does them, with an edge of challenge
alternatives: since you do these things, with no challenge
decisions.reason: The brothers do not doubt that Jesus does works; the condition assumes it. But John adds at once that they did not believe in him (7:5), so the words also carry a challenge: if he is what his works suggest, let him prove it before everyone.

decisions.choice: openly
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced say "openly" here and in 7:13 for the same word, so the thread of the chapter shows. Literal supplies "known", which the Greek implies. Readable says "want to be known" and keeps "openly" for 7:13.

records.greek: οὐδὲ γὰρ οἱ ἀδελφοὶ αὐτοῦ ἐπίστευον εἰς αὐτόν.
records.gloss: For not even the brothers of him were believing in him.

L.5: For not even His brothers were believing in Him.

R.5: Even His own brothers did not believe in Him.

decisions.choice: for: John explains why the brothers spoke as they did
decisions.reason: The sentence is the narrator's comment on 7:3-4. The brothers' advice is not the advice of believers. "Not even" shows how far the unbelief reached: his own family was not convinced.

decisions.choice: were not believing in him: they did not yet trust him as the one sent from God
alternatives: they had never believed and never would
decisions.reason: The tense describes their state at that time. They knew of his works and wanted them shown, but that is not the believing John writes for (20:31). It did not stay so: after the resurrection his brothers are with the disciples in prayer (Acts 1:14), the risen Jesus appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), and James became a leader of the church in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:19; Acts 15:13). Compare Mark 3:21, where his family tries to take charge of him.

decisions.choice: own
decisions.reason: "His own brothers" brings out the force of "not even" (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: λέγει οὖν αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ὁ καιρὸς ὁ ἐμὸς οὔπω πάρεστιν, ὁ δὲ καιρὸς ὁ ὑμέτερος πάντοτέ ἐστιν ἕτοιμος.
records.gloss: Says therefore to them the Jesus, "The time the mine not yet is present, but the time the yours always is ready.

L.6: So Jesus says to them, "My time is not yet here, but your time is always ready.

R.6: Jesus answered, "It is not yet the right time for Me. But for you, any time is right.

decisions.choice: my time: the right moment, set by the Father, for Jesus to act and to be revealed
alternatives: the hour of his death only
simply the right day to travel
decisions.reason: καιρὸς means the fitting or appointed moment rather than a span of time. It is a different word from "hour", which John uses for the hour of Jesus's death and glory (2:4; 7:30; 8:20; 12:23; 13:1), but the thought is close: as at Cana (2:4), Jesus will not act on someone else's timing. Here the nearest sense is the time to go up and show himself publicly, but the words look further, to the time when he will be revealed to the world on the cross and in his rising.

decisions.choice: your time is always ready: the brothers have nothing to wait for
decisions.reason: They may go to the festival whenever they like, because nothing hangs on it and the world has no quarrel with them (7:7). Jesus lives by the Father's timing (5:19, 30); they do not.

decisions.choice: not yet: the time will come
decisions.reason: "Not yet" points ahead. The same words return in 7:8 and in the narrator's remark that his hour had not yet come (7:30; 8:20).

decisions.choice: told (B); answered (R)
decisions.reason: John often tells a story in the present tense ("says") for vividness. Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, as stories are normally told in this language. This applies to every such verb in the passage.

decisions.choice: time (L, B, R); the right time (R)
decisions.reason: "Time" at every level, never "hour", so a reader can tell this word from the one the book's terms render "hour" (2:4; 7:30). Readable says "the right time" to show that a fitting moment is meant (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: οὐ δύναται ὁ κόσμος μισεῖν ὑμᾶς, ἐμὲ δὲ μισεῖ, ὅτι ἐγὼ μαρτυρῶ περὶ αὐτοῦ ὅτι τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ πονηρά ἐστιν.
records.gloss: Not is able the world to hate you, but me it hates, because I testify about it that the works of it evil are.

L.7: The world cannot hate you, but it hates Me, because I testify about it that its works are evil.

R.7: The world has no reason to hate you. But it hates Me, because I keep telling it that the things it does are evil.

decisions.choice: the world: humanity organized against God
alternatives: people at large, the public (as in 7:4)
decisions.reason: In 7:4 the brothers meant the public. Jesus takes up the word in its darker sense: people as they turn away from God and resist the light (1:10; 3:19-20; 15:18-19; 17:14). The world cannot hate the brothers because they belong to it; they share its outlook.

decisions.choice: I testify that its works are evil: his witness exposes what the world does
decisions.reason: Testimony is one of John's great themes (1:7; 5:31-39). The thought matches 3:19-20: people love darkness because their works are evil, and they hate the light that shows it. The brothers asked Jesus to show his works to the world (7:3); he answers that his witness shows up the world's works.

decisions.choice: cannot hate you: there is no reason for it to
alternatives: the world is unable to hate anyone good
decisions.reason: "Cannot" does not mean the brothers are good; it means the world sees nothing in them to oppose. Jesus says the same to his disciples in reverse: because he chose them out of the world, the world hates them (15:19).

decisions.choice: I keep telling it ... the things it does
decisions.reason: Readable uses the present of ongoing action for "testify" and says "the things it does" for "its works", matching 7:3 at that level.

records.greek: ὑμεῖς ἀνάβητε εἰς τὴν ἑορτήν· ἐγὼ οὐκ ἀναβαίνω εἰς τὴν ἑορτὴν ταύτην, ὅτι ὁ ἐμὸς καιρὸς οὔπω πεπλήρωται.
records.gloss: You go up to the feast; I not am going up to the feast this, because the my time not yet has been fulfilled."

L.8: You go up to the feast. I am not going up to this feast, because My time has not yet been fulfilled."

R.8: You go up to Jerusalem for the festival. I am not going to this festival, because it is not yet the right time for Me."

decisions.choice: I am not going up (SBLGNT)
alternatives: I am not yet going up (many manuscripts, including P66, P75 and Vaticanus)
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT reads οὐκ, "not". Many manuscripts, among them the early papyri P66 and P75 and Codex Vaticanus, read οὔπω, "not yet", the word used at the end of the verse. "Not" is found in Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Bezae and early Latin and Syriac versions. Because "not" seems to clash with 7:10, where Jesus does go up, it is easy to see why a copyist would change it to "not yet" and hard to see why anyone would change "not yet" to "not"; this is why the SBLGNT prefers it. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: I am not going up: not now, and not in the way the brothers ask
decisions.reason: Jesus goes up a few days later (7:10), so his words are not a flat refusal for all time. Three explanations are given, and they can stand together. First, the present tense means "I am not going up now", with his brothers' party. Second, he refuses the public display they asked for (7:4); when he does go, it is not publicly but as it were in secret (7:10). Third, "go up" is also John's word for Jesus going up to the Father (3:13; 6:62; 20:17): at this feast he will not "go up" in that sense, for his time is not yet fulfilled. The text does not say which is uppermost.

decisions.choice: go up: travel to Jerusalem for the festival
decisions.reason: Jerusalem stands on high ground, and pilgrims spoke of going up to it for the feasts (Psalm 122:4; John 2:13; 5:1).

decisions.choice: has not yet been fulfilled: the time is not yet full
decisions.reason: The verb pictures a measure being filled up: the time the Father has set is not yet complete. It echoes "not yet" in 7:6.

decisions.choice: has not yet fully come (B); it is not yet the right time for me (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the idea of fullness in everyday words; Readable says it as in 7:6. Literal keeps "fulfilled". Balanced and Readable say "festival", as in 7:2.

decisions.choice: to Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Readable names the place that "go up" implies (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: ταῦτα δὲ εἰπὼν αὐτὸς ἔμεινεν ἐν τῇ Γαλιλαίᾳ.
records.gloss: These things and having said, he remained in the Galilee.

L.9: And having said these things, He Himself remained in Galilee.

R.9: After Jesus said this, He stayed in Galilee.

decisions.choice: he himself: Jesus, in contrast to his brothers
alternatives: having said these things to them (some manuscripts)
decisions.reason: The pronoun is stressed: the brothers go, but Jesus stays. Some manuscripts read "to them" ("having said these things to them") instead; the sense is not changed. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: remained: stayed on, in the ordinary sense
decisions.reason: This is John's verb "remain", but here it has its everyday sense of staying in a place (as in 1:39 and 2:12), not the deeper sense of remaining in Jesus (6:56; 15:4).

decisions.choice: stayed on (B); stayed (R)
decisions.reason: The book's terms keep "remain" for the theological sense and use the natural word in ordinary senses. Literal keeps "remained".

records.greek: Ὡς δὲ ἀνέβησαν οἱ ἀδελφοὶ αὐτοῦ εἰς τὴν ἑορτήν, τότε καὶ αὐτὸς ἀνέβη, οὐ φανερῶς ἀλλὰ ὡς ἐν κρυπτῷ.
records.gloss: But when went up the brothers of him to the feast, then also he went up, not openly but as in secret.

L.10: But when His brothers had gone up to the feast, then He also went up, not publicly but as [it were] in secret.

R.10: But after His brothers had left for the festival, Jesus went too. He did not travel where people could see Him. He went almost in secret.

decisions.choice: as it were in secret (SBLGNT)
alternatives: in secret (some witnesses, among them Sinaiticus and Bezae)
decisions.reason: Most manuscripts, among them P66, P75 and Codex Vaticanus, have the small word "as", which softens the phrase: he went more or less in secret. Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Bezae and some early Latin copies leave it out, reading simply "in secret". Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: not publicly but in secret: the opposite of what the brothers asked
decisions.reason: "Publicly" is from the same root as "show yourself" in 7:4, and "in secret" repeats the brothers' own phrase. They told him that no one acts in secret who wants to be known; he goes up, but not to show himself to the world.

decisions.choice: then he also went up: on his own timing, not at his brothers' bidding
decisions.reason: Going up after the brothers is not a broken word (see the note at 7:8). As at Cana, where Jesus first said his hour had not come and then acted (2:4-7), he acts when the Father's time allows, and in his own way. In the middle of the feast he will teach openly in the temple (7:14, 26).

decisions.choice: publicly
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep "openly" for the different word of 7:4 and 7:13, and say "publicly" here so the two words stay distinct.

decisions.choice: He did not travel where people could see him. He went almost in secret.
decisions.reason: Readable spells out "not publicly" in a short sentence and gives the softening "as it were" as "almost".

records.greek: οἱ οὖν Ἰουδαῖοι ἐζήτουν αὐτὸν ἐν τῇ ἑορτῇ καὶ ἔλεγον· Ποῦ ἐστιν ἐκεῖνος;
records.gloss: The therefore Jews were seeking him at the feast and were saying, "Where is that one?"

L.11: So the Jews were seeking Him at the feast and were saying, "Where is that one?"

R.11: At the festival the Jewish leaders kept looking for Jesus. They kept asking, "Where is that man?"

decisions.choice: the Jews: the religious authorities in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: They are distinct from the crowds of 7:12, who are afraid of them (7:13), and their search picks up 7:1, where they were seeking to kill him. It is the leadership, not the Jewish people as a whole: the pilgrims at the feast are Jews too.

decisions.choice: that one: they avoid using his name
decisions.reason: ἐκεῖνος; is a pointing word, "that one". Their not naming him keeps him at a distance and may carry contempt (compare 9:12, 28).

decisions.choice: were seeking him: a hostile search
decisions.reason: The tense pictures a search that went on during the feast. John uses the same verb for seeking to kill Jesus (5:18; 7:1, 19, 25); in 7:34-36 Jesus will tell them that they will seek him and not find him.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: that man
decisions.reason: "That man" carries the same distance as the Greek in natural English. Literal keeps "that one".

records.greek: καὶ γογγυσμὸς περὶ αὐτοῦ ἦν πολὺς ἐν τοῖς ὄχλοις· οἱ μὲν ἔλεγον ὅτι Ἀγαθός ἐστιν, ἄλλοι δὲ ἔλεγον· Οὔ, ἀλλὰ πλανᾷ τὸν ὄχλον.
records.gloss: And muttering about him there was much among the crowds; some were saying, "Good he is," but others were saying, "No, but he leads astray the crowd."

L.12: And there was much muttering about Him among the crowds. Some were saying, "He is good," but others were saying, "No, rather He leads the crowd astray."

R.12: People in the crowds were whispering about Him. Some said, "He is a good man." Others said, "No, He is fooling the people and leading them away from God."

decisions.choice: muttering: low-voiced talk among the people
decisions.reason: γογγυσμὸς is the noun from the verb for the grumbling of 6:41 and 6:43, which echoes Israel's grumbling in the wilderness. Here the talk is not all complaint, since some speak in Jesus's favor: it is talk under the breath, kept quiet for fear (7:13). In 7:32 the Pharisees hear the crowd muttering these things.

decisions.choice: he leads the crowd astray: the charge against a false prophet
alternatives: an ordinary charge of misleading people
decisions.reason: πλανᾷ means to lead astray or deceive. Deuteronomy 13:1-11 warns against a prophet who does signs and wonders but leads the people away from the LORD, and orders that such a person be put to death. The charge is serious: it would make Jesus deserving of death. The Pharisees use the same verb in 7:47, and in Matthew 27:63 the chief priests call Jesus "that deceiver".

decisions.choice: he is good: an honest and upright man
decisions.reason: The verdict is favorable but limited: a good man, not the Christ or the prophet. It is not the believing John is calling for, and in 7:13 even these people keep their opinion quiet.

decisions.choice: among the crowds: the many groups of pilgrims at the feast
decisions.reason: The plural pictures the city full of pilgrims from many places. The singular "the crowd" at the end of the verse speaks of the people in general.

decisions.choice: muttering (L, B); whispering (R)
decisions.reason: "Grumbling" in 6:41 fit people who were complaining; here the talk includes praise, so Literal and Balanced say "muttering", which keeps the sound of the word and its link with 6:41 without implying that all of it was complaint. Readable says "whispering".

decisions.choice: is leading the people astray (B); is fooling the people and leading them away from God (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced says "the people", since the crowd as a whole is meant. Readable explains what leading astray means in this charge: turning people away from God (meaning decision m2). Literal keeps "leads the crowd astray".

records.greek: οὐδεὶς μέντοι παρρησίᾳ ἐλάλει περὶ αὐτοῦ διὰ τὸν φόβον τῶν Ἰουδαίων.
records.gloss: No one however openly was speaking about him because of the fear of the Jews.

L.13: However, no one was speaking openly about Him because of the fear of the Jews.

R.13: But no one dared to talk about Him openly, because they were afraid of the Jewish leaders.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the religious authorities in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: The people who are afraid are themselves Jews, so the word cannot mean the Jewish people here. It means those in power, as in 7:11 and in the other places where people fear "the Jews": the parents of the man born blind (9:22), the rulers who believed in secret (12:42), Joseph of Arimathea (19:38), and the disciples after the crucifixion (20:19).

decisions.choice: openly: freely and in public
decisions.reason: παρρησίᾳ is the word the brothers used in 7:4. They told Jesus to be known openly; instead, no one dares even to speak of him openly. Both his friends and his opponents speak under their breath (7:12).

decisions.choice: the fear of the Jews: the fear people had of the authorities
alternatives: the fear felt by the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: The phrase means the people's fear of the leaders, not a fear the leaders felt. The tense of "was speaking" describes how things stood throughout the feast.

decisions.choice: they were afraid of the Jewish leaders
alternatives: because of the fear of the Jews (Literal)
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote. Balanced and Readable turn "the fear of" into a verb, which is the natural way to say it.

records.greek: Ἤδη δὲ τῆς ἑορτῆς μεσούσης ἀνέβη Ἰησοῦς εἰς τὸ ἱερὸν καὶ ἐδίδασκεν.
records.gloss: Already but of the feast being at [its] middle went up Jesus into the temple and was teaching.

L.14: Now when the feast was already at its middle, Jesus went up into the temple and was teaching.

R.14: When the festival was about half over, Jesus went up to the temple courts and began to teach there.

decisions.choice: the middle of the feast: about halfway through the Festival of Tabernacles
decisions.reason: The festival is Tabernacles (7:2), which lasted seven days, with a solemn assembly on the eighth (Leviticus 23:34-36; Deuteronomy 16:13-15). Halfway through would be about the fourth day. Jesus had come up to Jerusalem quietly (7:10); now he teaches in public, in the place where the crowds gathered, while the authorities are looking for him (7:11).

decisions.choice: the temple: the whole temple area with its courts
decisions.reason: John has two words for the temple. This one covers the whole complex, with its open courts and colonnades where teachers taught and crowds could gather (10:23; 18:20). The sanctuary, which only priests entered, has a different word (2:19-21).

decisions.choice: was teaching: began to teach and went on teaching
decisions.reason: The imperfect tense describes teaching that went on over time. John gives none of the content here; the next verses report what people made of it.

decisions.choice: temple courts
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the courts, so that no reader pictures Jesus inside the sanctuary (meaning decision m2). Literal keeps the single word, as it does throughout John.

decisions.choice: the festival was half over (B); about half over (R)
alternatives: the feast being in the middle (Literal)
decisions.reason: Everyday English for the middle of a festival of several days; "festival" is the ordinary word for a feast day of this kind, as at 5:1.

records.heading: Teaching at the festival

records.greek: ἐθαύμαζον οὖν οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι λέγοντες· Πῶς οὗτος γράμματα οἶδεν μὴ μεμαθηκώς;
records.gloss: Were marveling therefore the Jews saying, "How this [man] letters knows not having learned?"

L.15: So the Jews were marveling, saying, "How does this [man] know letters, not having studied?"

R.15: The Jewish leaders were amazed. "This man never studied with any teacher," they said. "How does He know so much about the Scriptures?"

decisions.choice: the Jews: most likely the religious authorities in Jerusalem
alternatives: the Jewish people at the festival in general
decisions.reason: In this chapter the word first means the authorities: they want to kill Jesus (7:1), they look for him at the festival (7:11), and the crowd is afraid of them (7:13). Jesus answers these people (7:16) and asks why they are trying to kill him (7:19); the crowd, which knows nothing of a plot, then speaks up separately (7:20). The other reading is possible, since Jesus is teaching in public and anyone could have been amazed. A footnote gives it.

decisions.choice: letters: learning, especially in the Scriptures
alternatives: the ability to read and write
decisions.reason: The word means the letters of the alphabet, and from that, writings and learning. Jesus is teaching in the temple, so the question is how he knows the Scriptures and their meaning well enough to teach them. Moses' "writings" are called by the same word in 5:47. The question is not whether he can read.

decisions.choice: not having studied: not trained under a recognized teacher
decisions.reason: A teacher of the law was expected to have studied for years with a known rabbi and to pass on what he had received. Jesus had no such teacher (compare Acts 4:13 of Peter and John). The next verse answers this exactly: Jesus does have a teacher, the one who sent him.

decisions.choice: were marveling ... this [man]: astonishment with an edge of disapproval
decisions.reason: The same verb can describe admiration or shocked surprise (5:28; 7:21). Here "this man", said without his name, and the rest of the scene suggest the authorities are puzzled and suspicious rather than won over.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: The book-wide rule for John: Literal always says "the Jews"; Balanced and Readable name the group meant, here the authorities (meaning decision m1). A footnote gives the other reading.

decisions.choice: the Scriptures (B, R); under a teacher (B); with any teacher (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what kind of learning is meant and what kind of study was expected (meaning decisions m2 and m3). Readable puts the fact first and the question second, to keep each sentence short.

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη οὖν αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς καὶ εἶπεν· Ἡ ἐμὴ διδαχὴ οὐκ ἔστιν ἐμὴ ἀλλὰ τοῦ πέμψαντός με·
records.gloss: Answered therefore them the Jesus and said, "The my teaching not is mine but of the [one] having sent me;

L.16: So Jesus answered them and said, "My teaching is not Mine, but [is] of the one who sent Me.

R.16: Jesus answered them, "What I teach does not come from Me. It comes from the one who sent Me.

decisions.choice: my teaching is not mine: Jesus does have a teacher, God who sent him
decisions.reason: This answers the charge that he never studied (7:15). The teaching is his because he gives it, but its source is the Father. John returns to this again and again: the Son does nothing on his own (5:19, 30), and speaks what the Father taught him (8:28; 12:49-50).

decisions.choice: them: the people who asked the question in 7:15
decisions.reason: The pronoun picks up the speakers of the previous verse. What follows, up to 7:19, is said to them.

decisions.choice: the one who sent me: God, described by his act of sending
decisions.reason: Jesus often speaks of God in John as "the one who sent me" (4:34; 5:24, 30; 6:38-39). A messenger's words carry the authority of the one who sends him.

decisions.choice: two sentences: not my own ... It comes from ...
alternatives: My teaching is not mine but his who sent me
decisions.reason: The Greek plays on "my" and "mine". Balanced and Readable split the contrast into two sentences so the paradox reads clearly without sounding like a contradiction.

records.greek: ἐάν τις θέλῃ τὸ θέλημα αὐτοῦ ποιεῖν, γνώσεται περὶ τῆς διδαχῆς πότερον ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐστιν ἢ ἐγὼ ἀπ’ ἐμαυτοῦ λαλῶ.
records.gloss: if anyone wills the will of him to do, he will know about the teaching, whether from the God it is or I from myself speak.

L.17: If anyone wills to do His will, they will know concerning the teaching, whether it is from God or I speak from Myself.

R.17: Anyone who truly wants to do what God wants will find out whether what I teach comes from God, or whether I am just speaking for Myself.

decisions.choice: wills to do his will: a settled choice to obey God, not only a wish
alternatives: happens to do what God wants
decisions.reason: The sentence uses the verb "to will" and the noun "will" side by side. The condition is the person's own intent to do what God wants. "His" is the one who sent Jesus (7:16).

decisions.choice: knowing the source of the teaching follows a willingness to obey God
alternatives: learning more facts settles the question
decisions.reason: Jesus does not offer credentials to answer 7:15. He says that someone who wants to do God's will is able to recognize God's teaching when they hear it (compare 8:47; 10:4).

decisions.choice: I speak from myself: I speak on my own authority, as my own source
decisions.reason: The phrase is used in John for acting or speaking as one's own source rather than as one sent (5:19, 30; 7:28; 14:10). It is the opposite of what 7:16 has just said.

decisions.choice: {{gender:they|he}}
decisions.reason: "Anyone" includes men and women, so the pronoun that picks it up follows the gender setting.

decisions.choice: what God wants
decisions.reason: Readable names God instead of using a pronoun whose referent is a verse back (7:16).

records.greek: ὁ ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ λαλῶν τὴν δόξαν τὴν ἰδίαν ζητεῖ· ὁ δὲ ζητῶν τὴν δόξαν τοῦ πέμψαντος αὐτὸν οὗτος ἀληθής ἐστιν καὶ ἀδικία ἐν αὐτῷ οὐκ ἔστιν.
records.gloss: The [one] from himself speaking the glory the own seeks; the [one] but seeking the glory of the [one] having sent him, this [one] true is and unrighteousness in him not is.

L.18: The one speaking from themselves seeks their own glory; but the one seeking the glory of the one who sent Him, this [one] is true, and unrighteousness is not in Him.

R.18: People who speak only for themselves want glory for themselves. But I want glory for the one who sent Me. So I am telling the truth, and there is nothing false in Me.

decisions.choice: a general saying whose second half describes Jesus himself
alternatives: two general sayings about any teacher
decisions.reason: Both halves are worded as general rules. The first describes any teacher who is his own source. The second fits only the one who has just said that his teaching comes from the one who sent him (7:16), so Jesus is speaking of himself.

decisions.choice: glory: honor and praise
decisions.reason: Here glory is the honor a person seeks or receives. In 5:41-44 Jesus says he does not accept glory from people, and asks how those who receive glory from one another can believe.

decisions.choice: true: truthful and to be trusted
decisions.reason: The adjective describes a person whose word can be relied on (3:33; 8:26). It is not the noun for truth that John uses as a key word.

decisions.choice: unrighteousness: wrongdoing, here especially falseness
decisions.reason: The word means any kind of wrong. Set beside "true", it points to deceit: such a person is not trying to mislead anyone. It is the opposite of what is right, but not the noun for righteousness that is a key term.

decisions.choice: unrighteousness (L); nothing false (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the broad word. Balanced and Readable give the sense this context calls for (meaning decision m4).

decisions.choice: But I want glory for the one who sent me
alternatives: But whoever seeks the glory of the one who sent him
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly that the second half is about Jesus (meaning decision m1), and keeps the first half general.

records.greek: Οὐ Μωϋσῆς δέδωκεν ὑμῖν τὸν νόμον;
records.gloss: Not Moses has given you the law?

L.19: Has not Moses given you the law?

R.19: Moses gave you the law, did he not?

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer yes
decisions.reason: The negative at the start of the question expects agreement. The perfect tense means a gift once given and still in force.

decisions.choice: the law: the law of Moses, given at Sinai
decisions.reason: The law God gave Israel through Moses (1:17), which they honored and claimed to keep (5:45-47). Jesus's argument in 7:22-23 turns on two of its commands.

decisions.choice: Moses gave you the law, did he not?
alternatives: Did not Moses give you the law?
decisions.reason: Readable puts the statement first and the question after it, which shows that the answer is obvious.

records.greek: καὶ οὐδεὶς ἐξ ὑμῶν ποιεῖ τὸν νόμον.
records.gloss: And no one of you does the law.

L.19: And none of you does the law.

R.19: But not one of you obeys it.

decisions.choice: and: and yet
decisions.reason: The simple "and" joins two facts that do not fit together: they have the law, and they do not do it.

decisions.choice: none of you keeps the law: shown by their plan to kill him
alternatives: no one can keep the law perfectly
decisions.reason: The next sentence makes the point: the law forbids murder (Exodus 20:13), and they are trying to kill him. As 7:22-24 will show, they also judge him by a rule they themselves set aside for circumcision.

decisions.choice: keeps (B); obeys (R)
decisions.reason: "Doing" the law is the Greek way of saying keeping or obeying it.

records.greek: τί με ζητεῖτε ἀποκτεῖναι;
records.gloss: Why me are you seeking to kill?"

L.19: Why are you seeking to kill Me?"

R.19: So why are you trying to kill Me?"

decisions.choice: seeking to kill me: the authorities' plan, known since the healing on the Sabbath
alternatives: a threat from the whole crowd
decisions.reason: John has already said that the authorities were seeking to kill Jesus because he healed on the Sabbath and called God his Father (5:16-18), and that this is why he stayed away from Judea (7:1). The same verb is used each time. Jesus says it openly to those who asked about his learning (7:15-16).

decisions.choice: why: a real question that exposes them
decisions.reason: Jesus asks for their reason. Since they claim to keep the law of Moses, a plan to kill an innocent man condemns them by that law.

decisions.choice: trying to (B, R); So (R)
decisions.reason: "Seeking to" means trying to. Readable adds "So" to show that the question follows from the one before.

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη ὁ ὄχλος· Δαιμόνιον ἔχεις· τίς σε ζητεῖ ἀποκτεῖναι;
records.gloss: Answered the crowd, "A demon you have; who you is seeking to kill?"

L.20: The crowd answered, "You have a demon! Who is seeking to kill You?"

R.20: The crowd answered, "You are out of Your mind! Who is trying to kill You?"

decisions.choice: you have a demon: you are out of your mind
alternatives: a careful claim that he is possessed
decisions.reason: To say someone "has a demon" was a common way of calling him mad or raving; the two charges stand side by side in 10:20. It is an insult rather than a diagnosis (compare 8:48, 52).

decisions.choice: the crowd: festival pilgrims who do not know about the plot
decisions.reason: The crowd is different from the people who questioned Jesus. Many had come from elsewhere for the festival and knew nothing of a plan to kill him, so his question sounds absurd to them. Some people of Jerusalem did know of it (7:25).

decisions.choice: who is seeking to kill you?: a denial in the form of a question
decisions.reason: They mean that nobody is trying to kill him. The reader knows better (5:18; 7:1).

decisions.choice: You must have a demon (B); You are out of your mind (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the image with a word that marks it as an outburst. Readable gives what the insult meant (meaning decision m1), since a modern reader might take it as a literal claim of possession.

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη Ἰησοῦς καὶ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Ἓν ἔργον ἐποίησα καὶ πάντες θαυμάζετε.
records.gloss: Answered Jesus and said to them, "One work I did, and all you marvel.

L.21: Jesus answered and said to them, "One work I did, and you all marvel.

R.21: Jesus answered them, "I did one work on the Sabbath, and all of you are shocked by it.

decisions.choice: one work: the healing at the pool of Bethesda on a Sabbath
decisions.reason: Jesus last taught in Jerusalem when he healed the man who had been ill for thirty-eight years, on a Sabbath (5:1-9). That one act started the authorities' plan against him (5:16-18). Verse 23 confirms which work he means. John often calls what Jesus does "works" (5:20, 36; 7:3).

decisions.choice: marvel: amazement mixed with disapproval
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used of the authorities in 7:15. Here it is the shocked surprise of people who think Jesus broke the Sabbath.

decisions.choice: you all: everyone listening, the crowd and the authorities
decisions.reason: Jesus now answers the crowd that has just spoken (7:20), and includes all who had heard of the healing.

decisions.choice: on the Sabbath
decisions.reason: Readable names the day, which Jesus makes explicit in 7:23, so that young readers know which work is meant.

decisions.choice: work
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep "work", John's word for what Jesus does, so that the link with 5:17, 20 and 36 is visible.

records.greek: διὰ τοῦτο Μωϋσῆς δέδωκεν ὑμῖν τὴν περιτομήν οὐχ ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ Μωϋσέως ἐστὶν ἀλλ’ ἐκ τῶν πατέρων καὶ ἐν σαββάτῳ περιτέμνετε ἄνθρωπον.
records.gloss: Because of this Moses has given you the circumcision, not that from the Moses it is but from the fathers, and on Sabbath you circumcise a man.

L.22: Because of this Moses has given you circumcision (not that it is from Moses, but from the fathers), and on [the] Sabbath you circumcise a man.

R.22: So think about this. Moses gave you the command to circumcise baby boys. (It did not really start with Moses. It started long before him, with Abraham and his sons.) And you circumcise a baby boy even on the Sabbath.

decisions.choice: because of this begins verse 22 and introduces Jesus's answer (SBLGNT)
alternatives: it ends verse 21: you all marvel because of this
decisions.reason: The phrase can be read with the end of 7:21 ("you are all amazed because of it") or with the start of 7:22. The SBLGNT places it at the start of 7:22. Read that way, Jesus turns from their amazement to the case of circumcision, which explains why the healing should not shock them. Elsewhere John nearly always puts this phrase at the start of its sentence (5:16, 18; 6:65), which favors the SBLGNT, but the other reading is old and makes good sense. A footnote gives it.

decisions.choice: circumcision came from the patriarchs, and Moses gave it a place in the law
decisions.reason: God gave circumcision to Abraham as the sign of the covenant, for every male on the eighth day (Genesis 17:10-12), long before Moses. The law of Moses then repeated it (Leviticus 12:3). Jesus corrects his own words in passing, because the age of the command matters to his argument: it is older than the Sabbath law given at Sinai.

decisions.choice: circumcision was performed on the Sabbath when the eighth day fell on it
alternatives: they waited until the Sabbath was over
decisions.reason: When a boy's eighth day was a Sabbath, the circumcision was done that day, even though it was work. Jewish teaching later written down in the Mishnah (tractate Shabbat 18:3 and 19:2) allows this. A reviewer should check these references.

decisions.choice: a man: a human being, here a newborn boy
decisions.reason: The word means a person. Here it is the male child being circumcised on his eighth day; the same word comes back twice in 7:23.

decisions.choice: So consider this (B); So think about this (R)
decisions.reason: Following the SBLGNT, the phrase introduces the argument (meaning decision m1). Balanced and Readable say so in words that point ahead, since "for this reason Moses gave you circumcision" would suggest a reason the text does not give.

decisions.choice: the patriarchs (B); Abraham and his sons (R); a boy (B); a baby boy (R)
decisions.reason: "The fathers" are Israel's founding ancestors, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Balanced and Readable say who is meant, and say "boy" because circumcision on the eighth day was done to infants. This loses the repetition of "man" in 7:23, which Literal keeps.

records.greek: εἰ περιτομὴν λαμβάνει ἄνθρωπος ἐν σαββάτῳ ἵνα μὴ λυθῇ ὁ νόμος Μωϋσέως, ἐμοὶ χολᾶτε ὅτι ὅλον ἄνθρωπον ὑγιῆ ἐποίησα ἐν σαββάτῳ;
records.gloss: If circumcision receives a man on Sabbath so that not may be broken the law of Moses, with me are you angry because whole a man well I made on Sabbath?

L.23: If a man receives circumcision on [the] Sabbath so that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with Me because I made a whole man well on [the] Sabbath?

R.23: You circumcise a baby boy on the Sabbath so that you do not break the law of Moses. Circumcision deals with only one part of the body. But I made a man well in his whole body on the Sabbath. So why are you angry with Me?

decisions.choice: an argument from the lesser to the greater
decisions.reason: If the law allows a small act on the Sabbath to keep the law, it must allow a much greater one. Jewish teachers often argued this way. A later rabbinic saying uses the same comparison: if circumcision, which concerns one part of the body, sets aside the Sabbath, how much more saving a whole life (Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 85b). A reviewer should check this reference.

decisions.choice: so that the law is not broken: so that the eighth-day command is kept
alternatives: so that the Sabbath is not broken
decisions.reason: The law that would be broken is the command to circumcise on the eighth day (Leviticus 12:3). To keep it, they set aside the rest of the Sabbath. So even by their own practice, one command can give way to another.

decisions.choice: a whole man well: the whole person healed, as against one part of the body
decisions.reason: "Whole" sets the healing against circumcision, which concerns one part of the body. The man of 5:1-9 had been ill for thirty-eight years and was made well in every way. "Made well" is the phrase used of him in 5:6-15.

decisions.choice: angry: bitterly angry
decisions.reason: The verb is a strong one, used of bitter, lasting anger. It appears only here in the New Testament.

decisions.choice: a boy (B); a baby boy (R); a man entirely well (B); a man well in his whole body (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the repeated word "man". Balanced and Readable say "boy" for the infant (as in 7:22) and "man" for the healed man, who is a specific adult and needs no gender setting.

decisions.choice: Circumcision deals with only one part of the body
decisions.reason: Readable spells out the contrast that "whole" implies (meaning decision m3), and breaks the long question into short sentences.

records.greek: μὴ κρίνετε κατ’ ὄψιν, ἀλλὰ τὴν δικαίαν κρίσιν κρίνετε.
records.gloss: Not judge according to appearance, but the just judgment judge."
pieces: what things look like on the surface

L.24: Do not judge according to appearance, but judge the just judgment."

R.24: Do not decide things just by what you see on the outside. Judge fairly, and decide what is really right."

decisions.choice: do not judge: stop judging this way
decisions.reason: The present tense with "not" usually tells someone to stop doing what they are doing, or not to make a habit of it. Jesus does not forbid judging; the next clause tells them to judge rightly.

decisions.choice: according to appearance: by what is seen on the surface
alternatives: by a person's face or standing
decisions.reason: The word means what is seen. On the surface, Jesus did work on the Sabbath. Underneath, he did what the law itself makes room for, and greater.

decisions.choice: just judgment: the kind of judging the law requires
decisions.reason: Moses told Israel's judges to judge the people with just judgment, without partiality (Deuteronomy 16:18-19; Leviticus 19:15). Isaiah says the coming king from Jesse will not judge by what his eyes see but with righteousness (Isaiah 11:3-4). Jesus asks his hearers to do what their own law asks.

decisions.choice: just: right and fair
decisions.reason: The adjective describes a decision that is right and fair. It is related to the noun for righteousness but is not that key term; here it is about how a case is judged.

decisions.choice: just judgment (L); a judgment that is just (B); judge fairly ... what is really right (R)
decisions.reason: "Just" is the plain word for a fair verdict and keeps the link with Deuteronomy 16:18 (meaning decision m3). Literal keeps the Greek pattern "judge the judgment".

records.greek: Ἔλεγον οὖν τινες ἐκ τῶν Ἱεροσολυμιτῶν· Οὐχ οὗτός ἐστιν ὃν ζητοῦσιν ἀποκτεῖναι;
records.gloss: Were saying therefore some of the Jerusalemites, "Not this [one] is whom they are seeking to kill?

L.25: So some of the people of Jerusalem were saying, "Is this not [the one] whom they are seeking to kill?

R.25: Some people from Jerusalem itself said, "Is this not the man our leaders want to kill?

decisions.choice: the people of Jerusalem: those who live in the city, not the festival crowd
decisions.reason: John uses a word for the city's own residents, not the crowd of pilgrims at the festival. In 7:20 the crowd denied that anyone wanted to kill Jesus; these local people know better. What the authorities intend (5:18; 7:1, 19) is known in Jerusalem itself.

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer yes
decisions.reason: The question begins with the negative that looks for agreement: "This is the man, is it not?" The speakers are sure of who he is; what puzzles them is what follows in 7:26.

decisions.choice: they: the authorities who have been trying to kill him
decisions.reason: The verb has no named subject. The people speak of the leaders as a group apart from themselves, the same people whose plan John has reported at 5:18 and 7:1.

decisions.choice: the one (B); the man, our leaders (R)
decisions.reason: Literal brackets the word English needs after "this". Readable names who "they" are, as meaning decision m3 explains; the speakers themselves know who wants Jesus dead. Balanced says "out to kill" for a plan already under way.

records.heading: Is this the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}?

records.greek: καὶ ἴδε παρρησίᾳ λαλεῖ καὶ οὐδὲν αὐτῷ λέγουσιν· μήποτε ἀληθῶς ἔγνωσαν οἱ ἄρχοντες ὅτι οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ χριστός;
records.gloss: And look, openly he speaks, and nothing to him they say. Perhaps truly have known the rulers that this is the Christ?

L.26: And look, He is speaking openly, and they say nothing to Him. Can it be that the rulers have truly come to know that this is the Christ?

R.26: But look! He is speaking out where everyone can hear Him, and nobody says anything to Him. Is it possible that the leaders really have found out that this man is the Christ?

decisions.choice: openly: in public, plainly, without fear
decisions.reason: The word means speaking freely and in the open. It picks up a thread in this chapter: his brothers urged him to show himself openly (7:4), and no one spoke openly about him for fear of the authorities (7:13). Now Jesus himself does what others fear to do.

decisions.choice: a doubtful question: surely the rulers have not come to know this?
decisions.reason: The word that opens the question puts forward something the speakers hardly believe: "Can it be that...?" They are not saying the rulers accept Jesus. They are puzzled that men who want him dead let him speak, and wonder aloud if the rulers have changed their minds. 7:27 shows that they themselves reject the idea.

decisions.choice: the rulers: the leading members of the Jerusalem council
decisions.reason: The same word is used for Nicodemus, "a ruler of the Jews" (3:1), and in 7:48 the Pharisees ask whether any of the rulers has believed in him. They are the men with authority over the temple and the city.

decisions.choice: the Christ: the Messiah, the anointed king God had promised
decisions.reason: With the article the word is a title, not a name: the one God would anoint to rule, whom the people expected (1:20, 41; 4:25). The question is whether Jesus is that person.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}, {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:his|His}}, {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}}, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Christ or for God uses the deity_pronoun setting, including "me" and "my" when Jesus speaks of himself, and pronouns for the expected Christ, since John means Jesus (4:25). At the start of a sentence "He" or "My" is written plain. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}
decisions.reason: Where the Greek has "the Christ" as a title, every level writes "the" before the setting, so that the alternative reads "the Messiah" (see the book's terms). This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: our leaders (B); the leaders (R)
decisions.reason: "Rulers" can suggest kings. Balanced and Readable say plainly that these are the people in charge in Jerusalem (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: ἀλλὰ τοῦτον οἴδαμεν πόθεν ἐστίν· ὁ δὲ χριστὸς ὅταν ἔρχηται οὐδεὶς γινώσκει πόθεν ἐστίν.
records.gloss: But this [one] we know from where he is; but the Christ, whenever he comes, no one knows from where he is."

L.27: But we know where this [man] is from; but the Christ, when He comes, no one knows where He is from."

R.27: But we know where this man is from. Nobody will know where the Christ is from when He comes."

decisions.choice: the belief that the Christ would appear without anyone knowing his origin
alternatives: no one will know his family or birthplace
decisions.reason: The speakers hold a view that the Messiah's origin would be hidden until he appeared. It was not the only view: in 7:42 others say he must come from Bethlehem, David's town. Jewish expectation about the Messiah took several forms, and John reports this one as something some in Jerusalem said.

decisions.choice: irony: they know his earthly home, but not where he truly comes from
decisions.reason: They know he is from Nazareth in Galilee (1:45-46; 7:41, 52). John's readers know that he comes from the Father (1:14; 3:13; 6:38), and Jesus says so in 7:28-29. By their own test, the fact that they do not know his true origin fits his being the Christ.

decisions.choice: no one knows: present tense for what will be true when he comes
decisions.reason: The verb is present, "no one knows", stating a rule about the Christ's coming. The sense is that at his appearing no one will know where he is from.

decisions.choice: will know (B, R); origin (B)
decisions.reason: English uses the future after "when he comes"; Literal keeps the present of the Greek (meaning decision m3). Balanced says "origin" to avoid repeating "where ... from".

records.greek: ἔκραξεν οὖν ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ διδάσκων ὁ Ἰησοῦς καὶ λέγων· Κἀμὲ οἴδατε καὶ οἴδατε πόθεν εἰμί· καὶ ἀπ’ ἐμαυτοῦ οὐκ ἐλήλυθα, ἀλλ’ ἔστιν ἀληθινὸς ὁ πέμψας με, ὃν ὑμεῖς οὐκ οἴδατε·
records.gloss: Cried out therefore in the temple teaching the Jesus and saying, "Both me you know, and you know from where I am; and from myself not I have come, but is true the [one] having sent me, whom you not know;

L.28: So Jesus cried out as He was teaching in the temple, saying, "You know Me, and you know where I am from. And I have not come of Myself, but the one who sent Me is true, whom you do not know.

R.28: While Jesus was teaching in the temple courts, He called out in a loud voice, "So you know Me, and you know where I come from! But I did not come on My own. The one who sent Me is real and true. And you do not know Him.

decisions.choice: cried out: spoke aloud with solemn force
decisions.reason: John uses this verb for a public proclamation, not a shout of anger: John the Baptist cries out his witness (1:15), and Jesus cries out in 7:37 and 12:44. What follows is said for all to hear.

decisions.choice: a statement with irony: you know me and where I am from, so you think
alternatives: a question: do you know me, and do you know where I am from?
a plain statement that they do know his origin
decisions.reason: The words can be read as a plain statement, as a question ("Do you know me, and do you know where I am from?"), or as an ironic statement. Jesus grants what they said in 7:27, that they know where he is from, and then shows how little they know: he did not come on his own, and they do not know the one who sent him. The irony reading fits the turn that follows with "and yet". A question would make the same point less directly.

decisions.choice: true: real and reliable
decisions.reason: The adjective means genuine, the real thing, and also faithful to his word. It is used of God in 17:3, "the only true God". The one who sent Jesus is real and can be trusted, so Jesus is not a self-appointed messenger.

decisions.choice: you do not know him: they do not know God, who sent Jesus
decisions.reason: The speakers worship God in the temple, yet Jesus says they do not know him. John repeats the charge in 8:19 and 8:55; knowing the Father and knowing the one he sent go together (17:3).

decisions.choice: temple courts (B, R)
decisions.reason: The word means the whole temple area, where people gathered and teachers taught, not the sanctuary itself (see the book's terms).

decisions.choice: on {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} own; an exclamation for the irony (B, R); real and true (R)
decisions.reason: "Of myself" is stiff; "on my own" says the same. Balanced and Readable mark the first words as an exclamation to carry the irony (meaning decision m2). Readable adds "real" to show the sense of "true" here.

records.greek: ἐγὼ οἶδα αὐτόν, ὅτι παρ’ αὐτοῦ εἰμι κἀκεῖνός με ἀπέστειλεν.
records.gloss: I know him, because from him I am, and that one me sent."

L.29: I know Him, because I am from Him, and that one sent Me."

R.29: But I know Him, because I came from Him. He is the one who sent Me."

decisions.choice: I, in contrast to you
decisions.reason: The pronoun "I" is stated for emphasis, set against "you" at the end of 7:28: you do not know him, but I know him.

decisions.choice: I am from him: Jesus comes from God's own presence
decisions.reason: The words answer the question of where he is from (7:27-28). He comes from the Father, as 6:46 and 16:27-28 also say, and only one who is from God has seen him (1:18; 6:46). This is the origin the people do not know.

decisions.choice: and that one sent me: he himself sent me
decisions.reason: The pronoun "that one" points back to God with weight: it is God himself who sent Jesus. Coming from him and being sent by him are the two grounds of Jesus's knowing him.

decisions.choice: But (B, R)
decisions.reason: English shows the emphatic "I" (meaning decision m1) with "but". Readable breaks the verse into two sentences.

records.greek: ἐζήτουν οὖν αὐτὸν πιάσαι, καὶ οὐδεὶς ἐπέβαλεν ἐπ’ αὐτὸν τὴν χεῖρα, ὅτι οὔπω ἐληλύθει ἡ ὥρα αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: Were seeking therefore him to seize, and no one laid upon him the hand, because not yet had come the hour of him.

L.30: So they were seeking to seize Him, and no one laid [a] hand on Him, because His hour had not yet come.

R.30: Then some people tried to grab Him. But no one touched Him, because His time had not come yet.

decisions.choice: they tried: an attempt that did not succeed; the subject is not named
decisions.reason: The tense describes an effort under way. John does not say who "they" were: hostile people in the crowd, or those who spoke for the authorities. In 7:32 the authorities act formally by sending officers.

decisions.choice: laid a hand on him: arrested him
decisions.reason: To lay a hand on someone means to take hold of him by force. The same phrase comes again in 7:44, and 8:20 says the same thing in other words.

decisions.choice: his hour: the appointed time of his death and glorification
decisions.reason: Jesus has said that his hour has not yet come (2:4) and that his time is not yet here (7:6, 8). The hour is the time the Father has set for his death and return to glory (12:23; 13:1; 17:1). Until then no one can seize him; 8:20 says this again.

decisions.choice: took hold of (B); touched, time, some people (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what laying a hand on someone means (meaning decision m2). Readable says "time" for the appointed hour, as the book's terms allow, and "some people" for the unnamed subject (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: ἐκ τοῦ ὄχλου δὲ πολλοὶ ἐπίστευσαν εἰς αὐτόν, καὶ ἔλεγον· Ὁ χριστὸς ὅταν ἔλθῃ μὴ πλείονα σημεῖα ποιήσει ὧν οὗτος ἐποίησεν;
records.gloss: From the crowd but many believed in him, and were saying, "The Christ, whenever he comes, not more signs will he do than [those] which this [one] did?"

L.31: But many from the crowd believed in Him, and they were saying, "When the Christ comes, will He do more signs than this [man] has done?"

R.31: But many people in the crowd believed in Him. They said, "When the Christ comes, will He do more signs than this man has done? Surely not!"

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer no
decisions.reason: The question opens with the negative that looks for "no": the Christ could hardly do more signs than this man has. The speakers are close to saying that Jesus is the Christ.

decisions.choice: believed in him: a real but early belief
decisions.reason: John uses the same words for true faith (3:16) and for belief that does not yet go deep (2:23-25; 8:30-31). Here belief rests on his signs; it stands against the hostility of 7:30.

decisions.choice: signs: deeds that point to who Jesus is
decisions.reason: John calls Jesus's works signs because they show his glory and lead people to believe (2:11; 20:30-31). In Jerusalem he had healed the man at the pool (5:1-9), and others had seen his signs at the Passover (2:23).

decisions.choice: a tag question (B); an added "Surely not!" (R)
decisions.reason: English shows that a "no" is expected (meaning decision m1) with "will he?" at the end, or with a short reply. Literal keeps a plain question.

records.greek: Ἤκουσαν οἱ Φαρισαῖοι τοῦ ὄχλου γογγύζοντος περὶ αὐτοῦ ταῦτα, καὶ ἀπέστειλαν οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς καὶ οἱ Φαρισαῖοι ὑπηρέτας ἵνα πιάσωσιν αὐτόν.
records.gloss: Heard the Pharisees the crowd muttering about him these things, and sent the chief priests and the Pharisees officers that they might seize him.

L.32: The Pharisees heard the crowd muttering these things about Him, and the chief priests and the Pharisees sent officers to seize Him.

R.32: The Pharisees heard what the people in the crowd were saying quietly about Jesus. So the leading priests and the Pharisees sent some temple guards to take Him away.

decisions.choice: muttering: talking in low voices
decisions.reason: The verb means talk under one's breath. It can mean grumbling, as in 6:41, but here, as in 7:12, it is the crowd's quiet talk about whether Jesus is the Christ. The Pharisees hear the favorable talk of 7:31.

decisions.choice: the chief priests and the Pharisees: the council's leading members
decisions.reason: The chief priests were the high priest and the leading men of the priestly families who ran the temple. Together with the Pharisees among them they made up the Jerusalem council; John names the two groups together in 7:45, 11:47, 11:57 and 18:3.

decisions.choice: officers: the temple police serving the council
decisions.reason: The word means attendants or assistants. Here they are the men who kept order in the temple for the chief priests. They come back empty-handed in 7:45-46, and they arrest Jesus in 18:3, 12.

decisions.choice: temple police (B); temple guards, take him away (R); leading priests (R)
decisions.reason: "Officers" alone does not say whose officers these are. Balanced and Readable name their role (meaning decision m3). Readable says "leading priests" so that "chief" is not taken as a single leader.

records.greek: εἶπεν οὖν ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ἔτι χρόνον μικρὸν μεθ’ ὑμῶν εἰμι καὶ ὑπάγω πρὸς τὸν πέμψαντά με.
records.gloss: Said therefore the Jesus, "Yet time little with you I am, and I go to the [one] having sent me.

L.33: So Jesus said, "Yet a little time I am with you, and [then] I go to the one who sent Me.

R.33: Then Jesus said, "I will be here with you just a little longer. Then I will go back to the one who sent Me.

decisions.choice: a little while: the short time left before his death
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks of the time left before he is taken from them. He says the same to the crowd in 12:35 and to his disciples in 13:33 and 16:16-19. The officers have just been sent to arrest him, but the timing is his, not theirs (7:30).

decisions.choice: I go: I go away, return to the Father
decisions.reason: John uses this verb for Jesus's departure to the Father through his death and resurrection (8:14, 21; 13:3, 33; 16:5). He came from the one who sent him (7:29) and goes back to him.

decisions.choice: then (all levels); go away (B); go back (R)
decisions.reason: The "and" joins two stages: first a little time with them, then his going. English shows the order with "then", bracketed in Literal. Balanced says "go away" for John's word of departure (meaning decision m2); Readable says "go back", since he came from the Father (7:29).

records.greek: ζητήσετέ με καὶ οὐχ εὑρήσετέ, καὶ ὅπου εἰμὶ ἐγὼ ὑμεῖς οὐ δύνασθε ἐλθεῖν.
records.gloss: You will seek me and not will find, and where am I you not are able to come."

L.34: You will seek Me and will not find [Me], and where I am, you cannot come."

R.34: You will look for Me, and you will not find Me. You are not able to come where I am."

decisions.choice: where I am: the present tense for where he will be with the Father
decisions.reason: Jesus does not say "where I will be" but "where I am". He speaks of the Father's presence as his own place, where he belongs already (1:18; 17:24; also 12:26 and 14:3). The emphatic "I" is set against "you". Some readers also hear in the words his "I am" sayings; here the plain sense of place comes first.

decisions.choice: you will seek me and not find me: when it is too late
decisions.reason: They are seeking him now to kill him (7:1, 25, 30). A time will come when they look for him and he is gone. In 8:21 Jesus adds that they will die in their sin. He says the same words to his disciples in 13:33, but promises to come back for them (14:3).

decisions.choice: a possible echo of Wisdom's warning in Proverbs
decisions.reason: In Proverbs 1:28 Wisdom says that those who rejected her will seek her and not find her. The words are close, and John elsewhere presents Jesus in terms used of God's wisdom, but the passage does not quote Proverbs, and the echo may not be intended.

decisions.choice: search for (B); look for (R)
decisions.reason: "Seek" is less common in speech; Balanced and Readable use everyday words, as at 6:24. They repeat "me", which Literal brackets, and put "where I am" after the verb, the usual English order.

records.greek: εἶπον οὖν οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι πρὸς ἑαυτούς· Ποῦ οὗτος μέλλει πορεύεσθαι ὅτι ἡμεῖς οὐχ εὑρήσομεν αὐτόν;
records.gloss: Said therefore the Jews to themselves, "Where this [one] is about to go, that we not will find him?

L.35: So the Jews said to one another, "Where is this [man] about to go, that we will not find Him?

R.35: The Jewish leaders asked each other, "Where is this man planning to go, where we will not be able to find Him?

decisions.choice: the Jews: the authorities and those around them who oppose Jesus
alternatives: the listeners in the temple generally
decisions.reason: Jesus has just spoken to the officers sent by the chief priests and the Pharisees (7:32) and to those who seek him (7:34). Those who reply take his words as being about them, the ones who would be searching for him. In this chapter "the Jews" are the authorities who seek to kill him (7:1, 11, 13). They may include people in the temple who sided with them; it is not the people as a whole, since the crowd, the people of Jerusalem and Jesus himself are all Jews.

decisions.choice: they misunderstand: they think of a journey, he means his return to the Father
decisions.reason: Jesus spoke of going to the one who sent him (7:33). His hearers think only of places on a map, where he might go out of their reach. John often lets hearers take Jesus's words on the wrong level (3:4; 4:11; 6:52); 8:22 repeats the misunderstanding in a darker form.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

records.greek: μὴ εἰς τὴν διασπορὰν τῶν Ἑλλήνων μέλλει πορεύεσθαι καὶ διδάσκειν τοὺς Ἕλληνας;
records.gloss: Not to the dispersion of the Greeks he is about to go and to teach the Greeks?

L.35: He is not about to go to the Dispersion among the Greeks and teach the Greeks, is He?

R.35: Is He going to go to the Jews who live far away in Greek lands, and teach the Greeks? Surely not!

decisions.choice: a scornful question that expects no
decisions.reason: The question begins with the negative that looks for "no". The speakers mock the idea: a teacher of Israel would hardly leave the land to teach foreigners.

decisions.choice: the Dispersion among the Greeks: Jews living outside the land in the Greek-speaking world
decisions.reason: The word means "scattering" and was used for the Jewish communities living outside the land of Israel. "Of the Greeks" says where they were scattered: among the Greek-speaking peoples around the eastern Mediterranean.

decisions.choice: the Greeks: non-Jews, people of Greek language and culture
decisions.reason: "The Greeks" here stands for Gentiles in general, the peoples among whom the Dispersion lived. Some take it to mean Greek-speaking Jews, but the speakers have just named the Jews of the Dispersion; the further step, teaching the Greeks themselves, is the point of the scorn. In 12:20 the word is used of Greeks who came up to worship at the festival.

decisions.choice: irony: what they mock comes true
decisions.reason: The speakers mean the idea as an absurdity, but John's readers know that it happens: Greeks come seeking Jesus as his hour arrives (12:20-23), and he has other sheep to gather (10:16; 11:52). Through his disciples his teaching reached the Greeks.

decisions.choice: the Jews scattered among the Greeks (B); the Jews who live far away in Greek lands (R)
decisions.reason: "The Dispersion" is a technical term most readers will not know. Balanced and Readable say what it means (meaning decision m2). Balanced puts the expected "no" into "surely ... not"; Readable adds a short answer.

records.greek: τίς ἐστιν ὁ λόγος οὗτος ὃν εἶπε· Ζητήσετέ με καὶ οὐχ εὑρήσετέ, καὶ ὅπου εἰμὶ ἐγὼ ὑμεῖς οὐ δύνασθε ἐλθεῖν;
records.gloss: What is the word this which he said, 'You will seek me and not will find, and where am I you not are able to come'?"

L.36: What is this word that He said, 'You will seek Me and will not find [Me], and where I am, you cannot come'?"

R.36: What does He mean when He says, 'You will look for Me, and you will not find Me. You are not able to come where I am'?"

decisions.choice: word: saying; they ask what it means
decisions.reason: "What is this word" asks about the meaning of what Jesus said. The speakers repeat his words exactly as 7:34 has them, which shows they heard him clearly but cannot make sense of them.

decisions.choice: the repetition stresses their failure to understand
decisions.reason: John repeats the whole saying so the reader sees its weight. The question is left without an answer; the reader knows that he goes to the Father (7:33). Even the disciples later ask a similar question (16:17-18).

decisions.choice: What is this saying of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} (B); What does {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} mean (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek asks what this word is. Balanced calls it a saying; Readable asks what he means. Both repeat the words exactly as each level gave them in 7:34.

records.greek: Ἐν δὲ τῇ ἐσχάτῃ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ μεγάλῃ τῆς ἑορτῆς εἱστήκει ὁ Ἰησοῦς, καὶ ἔκραξεν λέγων· Ἐάν τις διψᾷ ἐρχέσθω πρός με καὶ πινέτω.
records.gloss: On now the last day, the great [day] of the feast, stood the Jesus and cried out saying, "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.

L.37: On the last day, the great [day] of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out, saying, "If anyone thirsts, let them come to Me and drink.

R.37: It was the last day of the festival, the most important day. Jesus stood up and called out to the people, "If anyone is thirsty, they should come to Me and drink.

decisions.choice: the last day, the great day of the feast: the close of the Festival of Tabernacles
alternatives: the seventh day, the last of the seven days of the feast
the eighth day, the closing day of solemn assembly
decisions.reason: The feast is Tabernacles (Booths), named in 7:2. The law sets seven days of the feast and then an eighth day of solemn assembly (Leviticus 23:34-36; Numbers 29:35). John does not say whether "the last day" is the seventh day or that eighth day; both were high points. The sense of the sentence is the same either way.

decisions.choice: thirst and drink: an invitation set against the water of the feast
decisions.reason: During Tabernacles, according to the Mishnah (Sukkah 4:9, written down about AD 200 and describing practice in the temple before its fall), a priest drew water from the Pool of Siloam each morning of the feast and poured it out at the altar. Tabernacles was also linked with prayer for rain and with Zechariah 14:8, 16-17, where living waters flow out from Jerusalem and the nations come up to keep the feast. Jesus's call also echoes God's invitation in Isaiah 55:1, "Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters", and his words to the Samaritan woman about living water (4:10-14). The connection with the water rite is likely but not stated by John.

decisions.choice: stood and cried out: a loud, public announcement
decisions.reason: Teachers usually sat to teach (Luke 4:20; Matthew 5:1). Here Jesus stands and cries out, the verb John uses for a solemn public declaration (1:15; 7:28; 12:44). It marks what follows as a proclamation to the whole festival crowd.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:his|His}}, {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Christ or for God uses the deity_pronoun setting, including "me" and "my" when Jesus speaks of himself and "you" when people speak to him. At the start of a sentence "He" is written plain. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: {{gender:them|him}} (L); {{gender:they|he}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Anyone" means any person, man or woman, so the pronoun that takes it up has the gender setting. Balanced and Readable say "should come" for the command form "let him come", which is stiff in modern English, and "is thirsty" for "thirsts".

records.greek: ὁ πιστεύων εἰς ἐμέ, καθὼς εἶπεν ἡ γραφή, ποταμοὶ ἐκ τῆς κοιλίας αὐτοῦ ῥεύσουσιν ὕδατος ζῶντος.
records.gloss: The [one] believing in me, as said the Scripture, rivers out of the belly of him will flow of water living."

L.38: The one who believes in Me, as the Scripture said, 'Out of his belly will flow rivers of living water.'"

R.38: It is just as the Scripture says: rivers of living water will flow from deep inside the one who believes in Me."

decisions.choice: a full stop after "drink" (7:37): the rivers flow from the one who believes
alternatives: a comma after "to me": "let him come to me, and let the one who believes in me drink"; the rivers flow from Christ
decisions.reason: The manuscripts have no punctuation, so the words can be divided two ways. The SBLGNT ends the sentence at "drink" and begins a new one with "the one who believes in me", which then names the person from whose inmost being the rivers flow. The other way joins "the one who believes in me" to the call before it: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me, and let the one who believes in me drink." Then the rivers flow from Christ himself, and the two lines balance neatly; 19:34, where water flows from his side, and the rock that gave water in the wilderness (Exodus 17:6; 1 Corinthians 10:4) are often brought in on that side. On the SBLGNT side, 4:14 says that the water Jesus gives becomes in the one who drinks "a spring of water welling up", and the sentence reads naturally as it stands. Both readings agree that the living water is the Spirit (7:39) and that its source is Jesus; they differ on whom "his" means in the quotation. We follow the SBLGNT; a footnote gives the other reading.

decisions.choice: belly: the inmost being of a person
decisions.reason: The word means the belly or womb, and in biblical Greek it often stands for the inner self, the place of a person's deepest life and feelings. The picture is of water pouring out from the very center of someone. On the SBLGNT punctuation "his" is the believer (meaning decision m1); on the other reading it is Christ.

decisions.choice: as the Scripture said: a summary of several passages, not one verse
decisions.reason: No Old Testament verse has these words. Passages that come close are Isaiah 58:11 ("like a spring of water whose waters do not fail"), Isaiah 44:3 (water poured on the thirsty land, God's Spirit poured out), Ezekiel 47:1-12 (a river flowing from the temple and giving life), Zechariah 14:8 (living waters flowing out from Jerusalem, read at Tabernacles), and the water from the rock in the wilderness (Exodus 17:6; Psalm 78:16). Jesus seems to gather the sense of these rather than quote one of them. Which passages are chiefly in mind is uncertain.

decisions.choice: living water: flowing water, and water that gives life
decisions.reason: "Living water" was the ordinary term for running water from a spring or stream, as against still water in a cistern. As at 4:10-14, Jesus uses it of the life he gives, and 7:39 says what it means: the Spirit.

decisions.choice: his, him: no setting
decisions.reason: The pronoun is left plain, with neither the gender setting nor the deity_pronoun setting, because either one would decide whom it refers to, the believer or Christ (meaning decision m1). Literal keeps "belly"; Balanced says "from deep within", which is what the word means here (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: rivers of living water will flow from deep inside the one who believes in me
decisions.reason: Readable turns the hanging phrase into a plain sentence and names the believer as the one from whom the water flows, following the reading the text adopts (meaning decision m1). The footnote there gives the other reading.

records.greek: τοῦτο δὲ εἶπεν περὶ τοῦ πνεύματος οὗ ἔμελλον λαμβάνειν οἱ πιστεύσαντες εἰς αὐτόν· οὔπω γὰρ ἦν πνεῦμα, ὅτι Ἰησοῦς οὐδέπω ἐδοξάσθη.
records.gloss: This now he said about the Spirit whom were about to receive the [ones] having believed in him; not yet for was Spirit, because Jesus not yet was glorified.
