L.39: Now He said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in Him were about to receive; for [the] Spirit was not yet [given], because Jesus was not yet glorified.

R.39: Jesus was talking about the Spirit. People who believed in Him would receive the Spirit later. At that time the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified. That would happen through His death on the cross and His return to the Father.

decisions.choice: for the Spirit was not yet (SBLGNT)
alternatives: for the Spirit was not yet given
for the Holy Spirit was not yet
for the Holy Spirit was not yet given
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT reads simply "for the Spirit was not yet". Many manuscripts add a word to make the sense plain: some read "given", some "holy" ("the Holy Spirit was not yet"), and some have both ("the Holy Spirit was not yet given"). The additions explain the short reading rather than change its sense (meaning decision m2). Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the Spirit was not yet: not yet given to believers
decisions.reason: John does not mean that the Spirit did not exist: the Spirit came down on Jesus at his baptism (1:32-33). He means that the Spirit had not yet been given to those who believe. Jesus later promises to send the Spirit after he goes away (14:16-17, 26; 16:7), and after the resurrection he breathes on his disciples and says, "Receive the Holy Spirit" (20:22).

decisions.choice: glorified: Jesus's death, resurrection and return to the Father
decisions.reason: In John, Jesus is glorified in his "hour", his death on the cross together with his rising and his return to the Father (12:16, 23-24; 13:31-32; 17:1, 5). Until then the Spirit could not be given (16:7). The word is the key term "glorify".

decisions.choice: the narrator explains, looking back
decisions.reason: This verse is John's own comment, as at 2:21-22 and 12:33: he tells the reader what Jesus meant. "Those who believed in him" are all who came to believe; "were about to receive" looks ahead from the time of the story to the giving of the Spirit after Easter.

decisions.choice: [given] (L); given (B, R)
decisions.reason: English cannot say "the Spirit was not yet" without seeming to deny that the Spirit existed, which John does not mean (meaning decision m2). Every level supplies "given", the sense the context requires; Literal puts it in brackets.

decisions.choice: That would happen through his death on the cross and his return to the Father.
decisions.reason: Readable says what "glorified" refers to here (meaning decision m3), since a young reader would not know. It keeps the word "glorified" itself.

records.greek: Ἐκ τοῦ ὄχλου οὖν ἀκούσαντες τῶν λόγων τούτων ἔλεγον· Οὗτός ἐστιν ἀληθῶς ὁ προφήτης·
records.gloss: Of the crowd therefore, having heard the words these, were saying, "This is truly the prophet";

L.40: So [some] of the crowd, having heard these words, were saying, "This is truly the Prophet."

R.40: Some of the people in the crowd heard what Jesus said. They said, "This man really is the Prophet God promised to send!"

decisions.choice: the Prophet: the prophet like Moses promised in Deuteronomy 18:15-18
decisions.reason: God promised Moses to raise up a prophet like him (Deuteronomy 18:15-18), and by Jesus's time some expected this Prophet as a figure of the last days (1:21, 25; 6:14). After the feeding, people said the same thing (6:14). Here the talk of water may have reminded them of Moses, who gave Israel water from the rock (Exodus 17:6), but John does not say so.

decisions.choice: some of the crowd were saying: ongoing talk among different groups
decisions.reason: "Of the crowd" means some of them; 7:41 goes on to others with other views. The verb "were saying" describes talk going on through the crowd, not one shout.

decisions.choice: these words: Jesus's call in 7:37-38
decisions.reason: The words that set the crowd talking are the invitation to come and drink and the promise of living water.

decisions.choice: the Prophet, with a capital
decisions.reason: As at 1:21 and 6:14, the capital shows that a particular expected figure is meant, not any prophet. Readable says who he is (meaning decision m1): the crowd's own term meant the Prophet God had promised, so this adds nothing they did not know.

records.greek: ἄλλοι ἔλεγον· Οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ χριστός· οἱ δὲ ἔλεγον· Μὴ γὰρ ἐκ τῆς Γαλιλαίας ὁ χριστὸς ἔρχεται;
records.gloss: Others were saying, "This is the Christ"; but some were saying, "Not for out of the Galilee the Christ comes?

L.41: Others were saying, "This is the Christ." But some were saying, "Surely the Christ does not come out of Galilee?

R.41: Other people said, "He is the Christ!" But some said, "The Christ is not supposed to come from Galilee!

decisions.choice: a question expecting the answer no, voiced with disbelief
decisions.reason: The question is shaped to expect "no": the speakers take it for granted that the Christ does not come from Galilee. The small word "for" ties it to the claim just made: "[He cannot be,] for surely the Christ does not come from Galilee?"

decisions.choice: from Galilee: where Jesus was known to come from
decisions.reason: Jesus was known as "Jesus of Nazareth" (1:45-46), a town in Galilee, and he had spent most of his time there. The objectors assume that this settles where he is from. Others in Jerusalem expected that no one would know where the Christ comes from (7:27); the crowd is divided even about what to expect.

decisions.choice: the Christ: the anointed king Israel was waiting for
decisions.reason: "Christ" means "anointed one" (1:41), the king from David's line promised in the Scriptures. Some think Jesus is the Prophet (7:40), some the Christ, and some reject both; John lays out the views side by side, and 7:43 sums them up as a division.

decisions.choice: the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}
decisions.reason: A title with the article, so every level writes "the" outside the span, as at 1:20.

decisions.choice: is not supposed to come from Galilee!
alternatives: Surely the Christ does not come from Galilee?
decisions.reason: Readable gives the answer the question expects (meaning decision m1) as a plain statement of what the speakers believed. Balanced keeps the question with "Surely".

records.greek: οὐχ ἡ γραφὴ εἶπεν ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ σπέρματος Δαυὶδ, καὶ ἀπὸ Βηθλέεμ τῆς κώμης ὅπου ἦν Δαυὶδ, ἔρχεται ὁ χριστός;
records.gloss: Not the Scripture said that out of the seed of David, and from Bethlehem the village where was David, comes the Christ?"

L.42: Has not the Scripture said that out of the seed of David, and from Bethlehem, the village where David was, the Christ comes?"

R.42: The Scripture says that the Christ will come from the family of King David. It says He will come from Bethlehem, the town where David lived."

decisions.choice: the seed of David and Bethlehem: the promises of a king from David's line
decisions.reason: God promised David that one of his offspring would reign after him for ever (2 Samuel 7:12-16; Psalm 89:4-5; also Isaiah 11:1). Micah 5:2 says that a ruler of Israel will come from Bethlehem, small among the clans of Judah. Bethlehem was David's home town (1 Samuel 16:1-13; 17:12). "The Scripture said" sums up these passages; it does not quote one verse.

decisions.choice: irony: the speakers are sure of where Jesus is from
decisions.reason: The speakers assume Jesus comes from Galilee and so cannot be the Christ. John does not tell of Jesus's birth; readers who know Matthew 2:1-6 and Luke 2:4-7, where he is born in Bethlehem, will hear the irony. John's own concern is that they judge his origin by the wrong measure: he comes from the Father (7:28-29; 8:14). The text itself does not say more than this.

decisions.choice: the seed of David: David's descendants
decisions.reason: "Seed" is the usual biblical word for offspring, a man's descendants (as in 2 Samuel 7:12).

decisions.choice: the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}
decisions.reason: A title with the article, so every level writes "the" outside the span, as at 1:20.

decisions.choice: family line (B); family of King David, the town where David lived (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "family" for "seed" (meaning decision m3) and keep the question as a statement the speakers expect everyone to grant: Balanced with "does it not", Readable as a plain statement. Readable says David "lived" there for "where David was", and calls him King David for readers who do not know him.

records.greek: σχίσμα οὖν ἐγένετο ἐν τῷ ὄχλῳ δι’ αὐτόν.
records.gloss: A division therefore happened in the crowd because of him.

L.43: So a division occurred in the crowd because of Him.

R.43: So the people in the crowd were divided into groups because of Jesus. They could not agree about Him.

decisions.choice: division: a split into opposing sides
decisions.reason: The word is used of a tear in cloth; John uses it of people who split into camps over Jesus (also 9:16; 10:19).

decisions.choice: because of him: Jesus divides people
decisions.reason: In John people are divided by how they respond to Jesus (3:19-21; 9:39). The crowd's split is not over a rule or a teaching but over who he is (7:40-42).

decisions.choice: divided into groups ... They could not agree about him.
decisions.reason: Readable names Jesus and spells out what a division was.

records.greek: τινὲς δὲ ἤθελον ἐξ αὐτῶν πιάσαι αὐτόν, ἀλλ’ οὐδεὶς ἐπέβαλεν ἐπ’ αὐτὸν τὰς χεῖρας.
records.gloss: Some now wanted of them to seize him, but no one laid on him the hands.

L.44: And some of them wanted to seize Him, but no one laid hands on Him.

R.44: Some of them wanted to arrest Him, but nobody took hold of Him.

decisions.choice: some of them: some of the crowd
decisions.reason: "Them" refers back to the crowd of 7:43. The officers sent to arrest Jesus (7:32) may have been among them; 7:45-46 shows they too did nothing.

decisions.choice: laid hands on him: arrested him
decisions.reason: To lay hands on someone means to seize or arrest them, as in 7:30.

decisions.choice: no one laid hands on him: his hour had not yet come
decisions.reason: John has just explained a similar failure: "no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come" (7:30; also 8:20). Here he does not repeat the reason, but the reader is meant to remember it: no one can take Jesus before the time the Father has set.

decisions.choice: take into custody (B); arrest (R)
decisions.reason: The verb means to seize, here with the aim of arresting him (7:30, 32). Balanced and Readable use the plainer words for an arrest.

records.greek: Ἦλθον οὖν οἱ ὑπηρέται πρὸς τοὺς ἀρχιερεῖς καὶ Φαρισαίους, καὶ εἶπον αὐτοῖς ἐκεῖνοι· Διὰ τί οὐκ ἠγάγετε αὐτόν;
records.gloss: Came therefore the officers to the chief priests and Pharisees, and said to them those, "Why not did you bring him?"

L.45: So the officers came to the chief priests and Pharisees, and those said to them, "Why did you not bring Him?"

R.45: So the temple guards went back to the leading priests and the Pharisees. The leaders asked them, "Why did you not bring Him here?"

decisions.choice: the officers: the temple police
decisions.reason: These are the officers the chief priests and Pharisees sent to arrest Jesus (7:32). They served the chief priests and kept order in the temple (18:3, 12). John does not say how long it was since they were sent; 7:32 seems to fall in the middle of the feast (7:14), and this is the last day.

decisions.choice: the chief priests and Pharisees: the leaders who sat on the council
decisions.reason: The chief priests were the high priest and the leading priestly families; with leading Pharisees they made up much of the Jerusalem council. John often names the two groups together as the ones who act against Jesus (7:32; 11:47, 57; 18:3).

decisions.choice: those: the chief priests and Pharisees
decisions.reason: "Those" points to the leaders just named, who question their officers.

decisions.choice: temple guards; leading priests
decisions.reason: Readable says what the officers were and avoids "chief priests", which a young reader may not understand.

records.heading: The leaders refuse to believe

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθησαν οἱ ὑπηρέται· Οὐδέποτε ἐλάλησεν οὕτως ἄνθρωπος.
records.gloss: Answered the officers, "Never spoke thus a man."

L.46: The officers answered, "Never has anyone spoken like this."

R.46: The guards answered, "We have never heard anyone speak the way He does!"

decisions.choice: Never has a man spoken like this (SBLGNT)
alternatives: Never has a man spoken as this man speaks
Never has a man spoken like this man
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT has the short reading, found in some of the earliest manuscripts. Many manuscripts read "Never has a man spoken like this man", and some add "as this man speaks". The longer readings spell out what the short one implies. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: a man: any human being
decisions.reason: The word is the general word for a human being. The officers mean that no one has ever spoken like this. The reader may hear more in it: John has shown that Jesus is more than a man (1:1, 14; 10:33).

decisions.choice: the officers came back without him because of his words
decisions.reason: Sent to arrest Jesus, the officers return empty-handed; what stopped them was the way he spoke. Their answer stands against the leaders' contempt in the next verses.

decisions.choice: {{gender:anyone|a man}}
decisions.reason: The word means any human being (meaning decision m2), so Literal has the gender setting. Balanced and Readable say "no one" and "anyone", which are already inclusive.

decisions.choice: We have never heard anyone speak the way he does!
decisions.reason: Readable says what "like this" points to: the way Jesus speaks.

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθησαν οὖν αὐτοῖς οἱ Φαρισαῖοι· Μὴ καὶ ὑμεῖς πεπλάνησθε;
records.gloss: Answered therefore them the Pharisees, "Not also you have been deceived?

L.47: So the Pharisees answered them, "You have not also been deceived, have you?

R.47: The Pharisees answered, "Do not tell us that He has fooled you too!

decisions.choice: deceived: led astray from the truth
decisions.reason: The verb means to lead astray. It takes up what some in the crowd said of Jesus earlier, that "he leads the people astray" (7:12). The law warned against a prophet who would lead Israel astray from the Lord (Deuteronomy 13:1-5); the Pharisees treat Jesus as such a man.

decisions.choice: a question expecting no, said with scorn
decisions.reason: The question is shaped to expect "no": "Surely you too have not been fooled?" The perfect tense asks whether they are now in a deceived state. "You too" puts the officers alongside the crowd the Pharisees despise (7:49).

decisions.choice: taken in (B); fooled, with he as the one who did it (R)
decisions.reason: Everyday words for being deceived. Readable names Jesus ("he") as the one who deceived them, which the passive implies, and puts the scorn of the question into a plain exclamation.

records.greek: μή τις ἐκ τῶν ἀρχόντων ἐπίστευσεν εἰς αὐτὸν ἢ ἐκ τῶν Φαρισαίων;
records.gloss: Not anyone of the rulers believed in him, or of the Pharisees?

L.48: Has anyone of the rulers believed in Him, or [any] of the Pharisees?

R.48: None of our leaders have believed in Him. None of the Pharisees have either!

decisions.choice: the rulers: the leading members of the council
decisions.reason: "Rulers" are the men who held authority among the people, the members of the Jerusalem council. Nicodemus is called "a ruler of the Jews" (3:1).

decisions.choice: irony: a ruler and Pharisee is about to speak up
decisions.reason: The question expects the answer "none", but at once Nicodemus, both a Pharisee and a ruler (3:1), speaks in Jesus's favor (7:50-51). Later John says that many even of the rulers believed in him, though they kept it quiet for fear of the Pharisees (12:42).

decisions.choice: a question expecting no
decisions.reason: As in 7:47, the question is shaped to expect "no". The Pharisees argue that if none of the leaders believe, Jesus cannot be what the crowd says.

decisions.choice: a single one ... a single Pharisee (B); two statements (R)
alternatives: Has any of the rulers believed in him, or of the Pharisees? (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced brings out the scorn of the question; Readable gives the answer the question expects, "none", as two plain statements and says "leaders" for "rulers".

records.greek: ἀλλὰ ὁ ὄχλος οὗτος ὁ μὴ γινώσκων τὸν νόμον ἐπάρατοί εἰσιν.
records.gloss: But the crowd this, the [one] not knowing the law, accursed are."

L.49: But this crowd, which does not know the law, are accursed."

R.49: But this crowd knows nothing about the law of Moses. They are under God's curse!"

decisions.choice: this crowd that does not know the law: the common people, looked down on by the learned
decisions.reason: The Pharisees devoted themselves to studying the law of Moses and keeping it in detail. They scorn the ordinary people, who had neither the time nor the training to do so, as ignorant of the law and therefore easily misled. Later Jewish writings show the same contempt from some teachers for "the people of the land", a phrase that in the Hebrew Scriptures simply means the population of the country. The words reveal the speakers' attitude; John does not share it.

decisions.choice: accursed: under God's curse
decisions.reason: The law pronounces a curse on anyone who does not keep its words (Deuteronomy 27:26; 28:15). The Pharisees treat the crowd's ignorance as a failure to keep the law and so place them under that curse. The irony is that in the next verses they themselves ignore what the law requires (7:51).

decisions.choice: the crowd ... are: a singular noun with a plural verb
decisions.reason: "Crowd" is singular but "are accursed" is plural: the Pharisees think of the crowd as so many people.

decisions.choice: the law of Moses; God's curse
decisions.reason: Readable says which law is meant and whose curse, both of which the Pharisees take for granted (meaning decisions m1 and m2).

records.greek: λέγει Νικόδημος πρὸς αὐτούς, ὁ ἐλθὼν πρὸς αὐτὸν πρότερον, εἷς ὢν ἐξ αὐτῶν·
records.gloss: Says Nicodemus to them, the [one] having come to him before, one being of them,

L.50: Nicodemus, the one who had come to Him before, being one of them, says to them,

R.50: Nicodemus was one of those Pharisees. He was the man who had come to see Jesus some time before. Now he spoke up and said to them,

decisions.choice: Nicodemus: a Pharisee and a ruler who had come to Jesus
decisions.reason: Nicodemus is the Pharisee and "ruler of the Jews" who came to Jesus by night (3:1-2). He appears once more, bringing spices for Jesus's burial (19:39). "One of them" means one of the Pharisees and rulers just mentioned; he is the answer to their question in 7:48.

decisions.choice: the one who had come to him before (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the one who had come to him by night
the one who had come to him by night before
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts read "the one who had come to him by night", and some combine the two ("by night, before"); a few leave out the description altogether. The longer readings recall 3:2 and 19:39. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: says (L); said (B, R)
decisions.reason: John tells this in the present tense ("says"), the historic present, as he often does. Literal keeps it; Balanced and Readable use the past, as English tells a story. This applies once in the passage.

decisions.choice: Jesus (for "him"); Readable: one of those Pharisees, spoke up
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Jesus, since "him" right after "them" could be unclear. Readable puts the description first in its own sentences and says that Nicodemus was one of the Pharisees (meaning decision m1); it does not add "by night", which is the variant reading (m2).

records.greek: Μὴ ὁ νόμος ἡμῶν κρίνει τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐὰν μὴ ἀκούσῃ πρῶτον παρ’ αὐτοῦ καὶ γνῷ τί ποιεῖ;
records.gloss: "Not the law of us judges the man if not it hears first from him and knows what he does?"

L.51: "Our law does not judge the person unless it first hears from them and knows what they are doing, does it?"

R.51: "Our law says we must first listen to a person and find out what they have done. Only then can we judge them. Is that not right?"

decisions.choice: our law: the law's demand for a fair hearing
decisions.reason: The law of Moses tells judges to hear both sides and judge fairly (Deuteronomy 1:16-17), and to inquire carefully before condemning anyone (Deuteronomy 17:4; 19:18). Nicodemus does not quote one verse; he appeals to what the law plainly requires. The irony is sharp: the men who have just said the crowd does not know the law (7:49) are ready to condemn Jesus without hearing him.

decisions.choice: judge: pass judgment, condemn
decisions.reason: The verb means to judge, and here to judge against someone. In the setting it means to condemn Jesus without a hearing.

decisions.choice: the man: the person accused, whoever it is
decisions.reason: The article points to the person on trial in any case. The words are general, about anyone accused, though Nicodemus has Jesus in mind.

decisions.choice: a question expecting no
decisions.reason: Like the Pharisees' questions (7:47-48), Nicodemus's question expects "no": the law does not do this. He turns their own way of speaking back on them.

decisions.choice: {{gender:person|man}}, {{gender:them|him}}, {{gender:they have|he has}}
decisions.reason: The law speaks of anyone accused, man or woman (meaning decision m3), so the gender setting applies. Balanced says "anyone" and Readable "a person", which are already inclusive; the pronouns that follow carry the setting.

decisions.choice: two statements and a short question
decisions.reason: Readable states what the law requires and keeps Nicodemus's appeal to his hearers in "Is that not right?", which matches the question's expected answer.

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθησαν καὶ εἶπαν αὐτῷ· Μὴ καὶ σὺ ἐκ τῆς Γαλιλαίας εἶ;
records.gloss: They answered and said to him, "Not also you from the Galilee are?

L.52: They answered and said to him, "You are not also from Galilee, are you?

R.52: They answered him, "Are you from Galilee too, like Him?

decisions.choice: are you also from Galilee: a sneer, not a real question
decisions.reason: The question expects "no" and is meant as an insult: "Surely you are not one of those Galileans too?" They are not asking where Nicodemus was born; they are lumping him with the Galilean Jesus and his followers from the despised crowd (7:41, 49).

decisions.choice: Galilee: a region far from Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Galilee lay to the north, away from the temple and the leading teachers of the law in Jerusalem. The leaders treat coming from there as a mark against Jesus and those who speak for him (7:41, 52).

decisions.choice: like him
decisions.reason: Readable adds "like him" to make the sneer plain (meaning decision m1): they mean that Nicodemus is taking the side of the man from Galilee.

decisions.choice: a Galilean
decisions.reason: Balanced brings out that they are labeling Nicodemus, not asking about his home town.

records.greek: ἐραύνησον καὶ ἴδε ὅτι ἐκ τῆς Γαλιλαίας προφήτης οὐκ ἐγείρεται.
records.gloss: Search and see that out of the Galilee a prophet not is raised."

L.52: Search and see that out of Galilee a prophet does not arise."

R.52: Look in the Scriptures and you will see that no prophet comes from Galilee."

decisions.choice: a prophet (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the Prophet does not arise from Galilee
no prophet has arisen from Galilee
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT reads "a prophet". The early papyrus P66, and possibly P75, has "the prophet", which would make the claim narrower: the Prophet like Moses (7:40) does not come from Galilee. Many later manuscripts also read the verb as "has arisen" instead of "arises". Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: no prophet from Galilee: a claim the Scriptures do not bear out
decisions.reason: The leaders speak as if Scripture settles the matter, but the prophet Jonah son of Amittai came from Gath-hepher (2 Kings 14:25), a town in the territory of Zebulun in Galilee (Joshua 19:13). Those who scorn the crowd for not knowing the law (7:49) overlook this; John leaves the irony for the reader.

decisions.choice: search: study the Scriptures
decisions.reason: The verb is the one Jesus used in 5:39, "You search the Scriptures". The leaders tell Nicodemus to look into the written word and see for himself.

decisions.choice: the Scriptures
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name what is to be searched, which the verb implies here (meaning decision m3). Readable says "comes from" for "arises".

records.greek: Καὶ ἐπορεύθη ἕκαστος εἰς τὸν οἶκον αὐτοῦ, Ἰησοῦς δὲ ἐπορεύθη εἰς τὸ Ὄρος τῶν Ἐλαιῶν.
records.gloss: And went each to the house of him, \v 1 Jesus but went to the Mount of the Olives.

L.53: [And each one went to his house,
L.1: but Jesus went to the Mount of Olives.

R.1: But Jesus went to the Mount of Olives, a hill just outside Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: the passage 7:53-8:11 is printed in the text, set off in brackets as a passage whose place in John is disputed
alternatives: leave the passage out of the text and give it only in a note
print it without any mark, as part of John
decisions.reason: The story of the woman caught in adultery is missing from the earliest manuscripts of John, among them two early papyri (P66 and P75), Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, and from the early versions in other ancient languages. The first manuscript known to have it is Codex Bezae, from the fifth century. In later manuscripts it is found here, but some place it after John 7:36, after 7:44 or at the end of the Gospel after 21:25, and one group places it in Luke, after Luke 21:38. Some manuscripts that have it mark it as doubtful. Its style and vocabulary differ from the rest of John: it names the scribes (verse 3) and the Mount of Olives (8:1), which John does not otherwise mention, and uses other words John rarely uses. Many hold that it is an old and true account of Jesus that was handed down outside John and later written into the Gospel at this point. The SBLGNT prints it here in double brackets. It is translated here in square brackets: the opening bracket at the start of 7:53 and the closing bracket at the end of 8:11 mark where the passage begins and ends. The evidence shows that the passage was not part of the earliest copies of John; it does not decide whether the events took place. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: each: each of those present in the scene before, who now leave for their homes
alternatives: each member of the council of 7:45-52 only
each person in the festival crowd
decisions.reason: In its place here the sentence closes the scene of 7:45-52, where the chief priests and Pharisees argued about Jesus. It also sets up the contrast with Jesus, who does not go home but goes out to the Mount of Olives. The sentence does not say who exactly is meant; it may have come with the story from wherever it was first told.

decisions.choice: the Mount of Olives: the ridge east of Jerusalem, across the Kidron valley
decisions.reason: The Mount of Olives faces the temple across the Kidron valley. This is the only time it is named in John, though the other Gospels often mention it. Luke says that in the last days in Jerusalem Jesus taught in the temple by day and spent the nights on the Mount of Olives, and that all the people came to him early in the morning (Luke 21:37-38). The likeness is one sign that this story comes from a tradition shared with the other Gospels.

decisions.choice: an opening square bracket at the start of 7:53, closed at the end of 8:11
alternatives: no brackets, with a note only
a heading over the passage instead of brackets
decisions.reason: The brackets show the reader where the disputed passage starts and ends (meaning decision m1). At Literal, square brackets also mark words supplied in English; inside the passage they keep that use, and only the outer pair, opening before 7:53 and closing after 8:11, marks the passage itself.

decisions.choice: a hill just outside Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Readable says what the Mount of Olives was, so that the reader knows Jesus left the city for the night (meaning decision m3).

records.heading: The woman caught in adultery

records.greek: Ὄρθρου δὲ πάλιν παρεγένετο εἰς τὸ ἱερόν, καὶ πᾶς ὁ λαὸς ἤρχετο καὶ καθίσας ἐδίδασκεν αὐτούς.
records.gloss: At dawn now again he came into the temple, and all the people were coming, and having sat down he was teaching them.

L.2: Now at dawn He came again into the temple, and all the people were coming [to Him], and having sat down He was teaching them.

R.2: Very early the next morning Jesus went back to the temple area. All the people came to Him, so He sat down and began to teach them.

decisions.choice: all the people: the ordinary people of the city, gathering in large numbers
decisions.reason: The word used here for "the people" is common in Luke (Luke 21:38) but rare in John, who uses it only twice outside this passage (11:50; 18:14) and usually speaks of "the crowd". "All" describes a large gathering, as people say "the whole town came".

decisions.choice: the temple: the whole temple area, with its courts
decisions.reason: The word means the whole temple area, where teachers met their hearers in the courts and colonnades (10:23), not the sanctuary, which only priests entered.

decisions.choice: he sat down and taught: the usual posture of a teacher
decisions.reason: Jewish teachers sat to teach while their hearers stood or sat around them (Matthew 5:1; 26:55; Luke 4:20; 5:3). The verbs for coming and teaching describe a scene in progress: the people kept arriving and Jesus was teaching when the scribes and Pharisees came in (verse 3).

decisions.choice: temple courts (B); temple area (R)
decisions.reason: As elsewhere in John, Balanced and Readable show that the word means the courts of the temple (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: [to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}] (L); to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} (B, R); Jesus, the next morning (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek says only that the people were coming; to Jesus is clearly meant, since he then teaches them. Readable names Jesus at the start of the scene and says "the next morning", following on from 8:1.

records.greek: ἄγουσιν δὲ οἱ γραμματεῖς καὶ οἱ Φαρισαῖοι πρὸς αὐτὸν γυναῖκα ἐν μοιχείᾳ καταλήφθεισαν καὶ στήσαντες αὐτὴν ἐν μέσῳ λέγουσιν αὐτῷ, πειράζοντες Διδάσκαλε, αὕτη ἡ γυνὴ κατελήφθη ἐπ᾿ αὐτοφόρῳ μοιχευομένη ἐν δὲ τῷ νόμῳ Μωϋσῆς ἡμῖν ἐνετείλατο τὰς τοιαύτας λιθοβολεῖσθαι σὺ οὖν τί λέγεις;
records.gloss: Bring now the scribes and the Pharisees to him a woman in adultery having been caught, and having stood her in [the] middle \v 4 they say to him, testing: Teacher, this the woman was caught in the very act committing adultery; \v 5 in now the law Moses to us commanded such [women] to be stoned; you therefore what do you say?

L.3: Now the scribes and the Pharisees bring to Him a woman caught in adultery, and having stood her in the middle,
L.4: they say to Him, testing [Him], "Teacher, this woman has been caught in the very act of committing adultery.
L.5: Now in the Law Moses commanded us [that] such [women] be stoned. You, then, what do You say?"

R.3: Then the teachers of the Law and the Pharisees came to Jesus with a woman who had been caught committing adultery. They put her in the middle, in front of everyone.
R.4: They were trying to trap Jesus, so they said to Him, "Teacher, this woman was caught while she was committing adultery.
R.5: In the Law, Moses told us to kill women like this by throwing stones at them. But what do You say?"

decisions.choice: the scribes: experts who copied, taught and applied the Law of Moses
decisions.reason: The word first meant a writer or clerk, but in the Gospels it names the experts in the Law, who often appear together with the Pharisees (Mark 2:16; Luke 5:21, 30). This is the only place where they appear in John, which elsewhere speaks of the chief priests and the Pharisees (7:32, 45).

decisions.choice: the Law commanded death for adultery, for the man as well as the woman
alternatives: the Law commanded stoning for the woman only
decisions.reason: The Law of Moses says that when a man commits adultery with another man's wife, both the man and the woman are to be put to death (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22). Where the woman was engaged to be married, it names stoning for both of them (Deuteronomy 22:23-24); for a married woman the method is not stated. The accusers speak only of "such women", and they bring the woman but not the man, though they claim she was caught in the act. The story does not say why the man is missing, and it does not say whether the woman was married or engaged.

decisions.choice: in the very act: caught while the act was taking place
decisions.reason: The phrase means "caught red-handed". The Law required two or three witnesses before anyone was put to death (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15), and the accusers stress that the facts are not in doubt.

decisions.choice: testing: in verse 4, and again in verse 6 (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the word about testing in verse 4 only
the word about testing in verse 6 only
decisions.reason: The manuscripts of this passage differ a good deal in wording. The SBLGNT has the word "testing" both here and in verse 6; some manuscripts have it in only one of the two places, and some put the whole comment about their aim in verse 4. The meaning is the same either way. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: you, then: an emphatic "you", set against Moses
alternatives: a plain question with no contrast
decisions.reason: The pronoun is written out, which the Greek does not need, and it stands first: Moses has spoken; what do you say? The question invites Jesus to say something that can be set against the Law.

decisions.choice: brought ... said (B, R)
decisions.reason: The historic present: the story tells past events with present-tense verbs ("they bring", "they say"), a lively way of telling a story. Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, which is normal in English narrative. This note covers the passage.

decisions.choice: the teachers of the Law
decisions.reason: "Scribes" today suggests people who only copy; Readable says what they were (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: [that] such [women] be stoned (L); kill women like this by throwing stones at them (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek says "such" in the feminine, so "women" is understood; Literal shows it in brackets. Readable says plainly what stoning was: a way of putting a person to death.

records.greek: τοῦτο δὲ ἔλεγον πειράζοντες αὐτόν, ἵνα ἔχωσιν κατηγορεῖν αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: This now they were saying testing him, so that they might have to accuse him.

L.6: Now they were saying this testing Him, so that they might have [grounds] to accuse Him.

R.6: They asked this to trap Jesus. They wanted a reason to bring charges against Him.

decisions.choice: testing: trying to trap him into saying something wrong
decisions.reason: The same verb can mean a fair test (6:6), but here, as when Jesus' opponents question him in the other Gospels (Mark 10:2; 12:15), the aim is to catch him out. The rest of the sentence says so.

decisions.choice: have to accuse: have grounds on which to bring a charge
decisions.reason: "To have" with a verb means to have the means or occasion to do it. They wanted something Jesus said that they could use as a charge against him.

decisions.choice: a trap: either answer could be used against him
alternatives: a sincere question about the Law
decisions.reason: The story does not explain the trap, but its outline is clear. If Jesus said that the woman should go free, they could accuse him of setting aside the Law of Moses. If he said that she should be stoned, he would go against the mercy he was known for, and he could also be accused before the Roman governor, since under Roman rule the Jewish authorities were not allowed to put anyone to death on their own (18:31). Whether the second danger was in view depends on how strictly that rule was kept in practice, which is not certain.

decisions.choice: [grounds] (L); a reason to bring charges (R)
alternatives: so that they might have to accuse him
decisions.reason: "Have to accuse" is not English; Literal supplies "grounds" in brackets (meaning decision m2). Readable names the testing as a trap (m1).

records.greek: ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς κάτω κύψας τῷ δακτύλῳ ἔγραφεν εἰς τὴν γῆν.
records.gloss: But Jesus down having stooped with the finger was writing on the ground.

L.6: But Jesus, having stooped down, was writing with [His] finger on the ground.

R.6: But Jesus bent over and used His finger to write on the ground.

decisions.choice: was writing: forming letters or words; what he wrote is not said
alternatives: writing the sins of the accusers
decisions.reason: The verb means to write. The story does not say what Jesus wrote, and nothing in it depends on the words; what matters is that he does not answer at once. Guesses about the words go beyond the text.

decisions.choice: no sure allusion
alternatives: an echo of Jeremiah 17:13, where those who turn away from the LORD are "written in the earth"
an echo of the Law written by "the finger of God" (Exodus 31:18)
decisions.reason: Some readers hear an echo of Jeremiah 17:13 or of the tablets of the Law written by the finger of God. The story itself points to neither, so the link is possible but uncertain.

decisions.choice: was writing: the imperfect describes action going on while they kept asking
decisions.reason: The tense pictures Jesus writing as the questions continued (verse 7).

decisions.choice: began writing
decisions.reason: Balanced shows that the writing went on (meaning decision m3); Readable keeps the plain past.

records.greek: μὴ προσποιούμενος ὡς δὲ ἐπέμενον ἐρωτῶντες αὐτόν, ἀνακύψας εἶπεν πρὸς αὐτούς Ὁ ἀναμάρτητος ὑμῶν πρῶτον ἐπ᾿ αὐτὴν τὸν λίθον βαλέτω καὶ πάλιν κάτω κύψας ἔγραφεν εἰς τὴν γῆν.
records.gloss: not paying attention. \v 7 As now they continued asking him, having straightened up he said to them, The sinless [one] of you first at her the stone let him throw. \v 8 And again down having stooped he was writing on the ground.

L.7: But as they kept on asking Him, having straightened up, He said to them, "Let the sinless one among you be first to throw the stone at her."
L.8: And again having stooped down, He was writing on the ground.

R.6: Jesus did not pay attention to them.
R.7: But they kept asking Him questions. So He stood up and spoke to them. "Any one of you who has never sinned may throw the first stone at her."
R.8: Then He bent down again and kept writing on the ground.

decisions.choice: the two words for "not paying attention" open this record, following the token data
alternatives: they close the previous sentence, as the SBLGNT prints them: "he was writing on the ground, not paying attention"
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT prints a full stop after these two words, so that they end verse 6 and describe Jesus as he wrote. The token data that these records follow puts the full stop before them, so they stand at the start of this sentence. The meaning does not change: either way Jesus is writing and does not respond to the questions. These two words are also missing from many manuscripts of the passage; others add to them, "as though he did not hear". A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: not paying attention: taking no notice of them
alternatives: as though he did not hear them
decisions.reason: The verb means to act as if or to take notice of something. With "not" it says that Jesus did not respond to them, but kept on writing.

decisions.choice: the sinless one among you: anyone of them who has not sinned
alternatives: one who has not committed this particular sin
one who is not guilty in this case
decisions.reason: The word means "without sin" in general. Jesus does not deny the Law or the woman's guilt; he turns the question to the accusers themselves. The words are masculine, since the accusers in front of him are men, but the principle he states is a general one.

decisions.choice: the stone, first: the first stone of an execution, thrown by the witnesses
decisions.reason: The Law said that at an execution "the hand of the witnesses" was to be first against the condemned person, and then the hand of all the people (Deuteronomy 17:7). The article points to the stone that begins the stoning. Jesus asks those who claim to be witnesses to take that first step, if they are without sin themselves.

decisions.choice: [He was] (L); He took no notice of them (B); Jesus did not pay attention to them (R)
decisions.reason: The two words are a participle with no main verb in this sentence (meaning decision m1), so every level makes them a short sentence of their own; Literal shows the supplied words in brackets.

decisions.choice: the sinless one among you (L); whoever among you has no sin, let that person (B); any one of you who has never sinned (R)
alternatives: let him who is without sin
he who is without sin among you, let him
decisions.reason: The Greek has a third-person command, "let him throw". English can carry it without a pronoun, so every level states the general principle (meaning decision m3) in words that already include everyone; no reader setting is needed.

records.greek: οἱ δὲ ἀκούσαντες καὶ ὑπὸ τῆς συνειδήσεως ἐλεγχόμενοι ἐξήρχοντο εἷς καθ᾿ εἷς ἀρξάμενοι ἀπὸ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων, καὶ κατελείφθη μόνος, ὁ Ἰησοῦς καὶ ἡ γυνὴ ἐν μέσῳ οὖσα.
records.gloss: They now having heard and by the conscience being convicted were going out one by one, having begun from the older ones, and was left alone Jesus, and the woman in [the] middle being.

L.9: And having heard [it] and being convicted by [their] conscience, they went out one by one, beginning from the older ones; and Jesus was left alone, and the woman, being in the middle.

R.9: When they heard what He said, their consciences told them that they were guilty. One by one they went away, starting with the oldest. In the end the accusers were all gone. Jesus was left with the woman, who was still standing in the middle where they had put her.

decisions.choice: and being convicted by their conscience (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the words are absent: "when they heard it, they went out one by one"
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT text includes the words about their conscience. They are found in many later manuscripts of the passage but missing from others, including some of the earliest that have the story. Some manuscripts also add, after "the older ones", "until the last". A footnote gives the shorter reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the older ones: the older men, by age
alternatives: the elders, members of the ruling council
decisions.reason: The same word is used for the elders who sat on the council, but here it is paired with going out "one by one" in order, so the order of age is meant. The oldest leave first, perhaps because they had the longest lives to look back on, though the story does not say why.

decisions.choice: left alone: without the accusers; the woman was still standing where they had put her
alternatives: no one else at all was left in the temple courts
decisions.reason: "Alone" means that the accusers had gone. The woman is still "in the middle", the place where they made her stand (verse 3), in the middle of the people Jesus had been teaching (verse 2), who may still have been there.

decisions.choice: they went out: the imperfect describes them leaving one after another
decisions.reason: The tense shows a process: the accusers went out over a short time, one at a time.

decisions.choice: In the end the accusers were all gone ... where they had put her
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly who had gone and why the woman was "in the middle" (meaning decision m3), so that "alone" does not seem to contradict the woman's presence.

records.greek: ἀνακύψας δὲ ὁ Ἰησοῦς καὶ μηδένα θεασάμενος πλὴν τὴς γυναικός εἶπεν αὐτῇ, ποῦ εἰσιν;; ἐκεῖνοι οἱ κατήγοροί σου οὐδείς σε κατέκρινεν;
records.gloss: Having straightened up now Jesus and no one having seen except the woman he said to her, Where are they, those the accusers of you? No one you condemned?

L.10: And Jesus, having straightened up and having seen no one except the woman, said to her, "Where are they, those accusers of yours? Has no one condemned you?"

R.10: Jesus stood up straight and saw that no one was there except the woman. He asked her, "Where did they go, all those people who were accusing you? Did not even one of them condemn you?"

decisions.choice: and seeing no one except the woman ... Where are they, those accusers of yours? (SBLGNT, with no word of address)
alternatives: "Jesus straightened up and said to her, 'Woman, where are they?'"
"... said to her, 'Woman, where are those accusers of yours?'"
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT text has the words "and seeing no one except the woman" and no word of address. Many manuscripts of the passage read differently: some lack the words about seeing no one, and many have Jesus address her as "Woman". The meaning is not affected. A footnote gives the other reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: one question: "Where are they, those accusers of yours?"
alternatives: two questions: "Where are they? Those accusers of yours?"
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT prints a question mark after "your accusers". The token data marks a question after "are they" instead (with the mark doubled, apparently an error in the data). Either way "those accusers of yours" names who "they" are.

decisions.choice: condemned: gave a verdict of guilty that leads to punishment
decisions.reason: The word means to pronounce someone guilty and pass sentence. No accuser stayed to bring the charge or to throw the first stone, so no sentence had been passed. The question expects the answer "no one".

decisions.choice: the people who were accusing you (B); all those people who were accusing you (R)
decisions.reason: "Accusers" is an uncommon word in speech; Balanced and Readable use the verb.

records.greek: ἡ δὲ εἶπεν, Οὐδείς, κύριε.
records.gloss: She now said, No one, sir.

decisions.choice: Sir: a polite address to a man
alternatives: Lord, a confession of who Jesus is
decisions.reason: The word is the one later used of Jesus as Lord (20:28), but it was also the ordinary courteous way to address a man. Nothing in the story shows that the woman knows who Jesus is. A footnote gives "Lord".

decisions.choice: Sir
decisions.reason: Shows the polite address (meaning decision m1); "Lord" would put in her mouth a confession the story does not report.

records.greek: εἶπεν δὲ ὁ Ἰησοῦς, Οὐδὲ ἐγώ σε κρίνω πορεύου, καὶ μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε.
records.gloss: Said then Jesus, Neither I you condemn; go, and no longer sin.

L.11: And Jesus said, "I do not condemn you either; go, and sin no longer."]

R.11: Jesus said, "I do not condemn you either. Go now, and from now on stop sinning."]

decisions.choice: condemn: pass sentence on, as in the previous verse
alternatives: judge, in the sense of forming an opinion
decisions.reason: The verb is the simpler form of the one in verse 10 and carries the same sense here: "Neither do I" answers "No one". Jesus does not pass sentence on her, in keeping with what John says elsewhere: God sent the Son not to condemn the world but to save it (3:17).

decisions.choice: no longer sin: a present command, to stop sinning and not go back to it
alternatives: a statement that she has not sinned
decisions.reason: The command assumes that she has sinned, and calls her to a changed life from now on. Jesus says the same words to the man he healed at the pool (5:14).

decisions.choice: mercy together with a call to leave sin
alternatives: a verdict that she was innocent
decisions.reason: Jesus neither denies her guilt nor approves of it. He sends her away without sentence, and he tells her not to sin again. Both parts belong to his answer.

decisions.choice: I do not condemn you either
decisions.reason: The more familiar wording puts "Neither" first, which is closer to the Greek order but is rarely spoken today; every level uses the plain form.

decisions.choice: a closing square bracket at the end of 8:11
decisions.reason: Closes the disputed passage opened at 7:53 (see the notes there).
